         Ruth Ballard, Ph.D. INC, may testify for the defense as an expert regarding Forensic

Biology/DNA. Ms. Ballard’s opinion/testimony will be based on her experience, education, and

trainings as detailed in her curriculum vitae which is included with this response as Exhibit D1-C.

         This response serves to supplement the information in the Report attached as Exhibit D1-

B. The below is a summary of Ruth Ballard’s anticipated testimony but does not repeat all specific

findings that are detailed in her report. It is anticipated that Ms. Ballard may testify in the following

areas:

         1. The Process of DNA Analysis, extraction, quantification, amplification.

         2. The STR testing done in this case including data interpretation and STR Mix Probabilistic

             genotyping to generate a statistical weight of the STR data.

         3. Lab testing standards and policy procedures.

         4. The findings, impressions, conclusions, and materials relating to forensic testing conducted

             in this case.

         5. The lack of testing conducted on samples collected in this case.

         6. DNA Transfer including the shedding of biological material by individuals, the deposition

             of those materials on objects, and the inability to age DNA from such deposits.

This disclosure is provided as a summary. For further detail on the scope and depth of her testimony

see her report and Curriculum Vitae. Dr. Ballard may offer additional testimony as necessary to meet

undisclosed expert opinion the State may offer.

BIOLOGY/DNA REPORT

Independent review of DNA discovery and other relevant documents/files in the case of
State v Bryan Kohberger; Idaho State Police Forensic Services Laboratory Case # M2022-
4843, BODE Case # CCA2401, and Cybergenetics Case BK.

Background qualifications

I am a human molecular geneticist with an expertise in forensic serology and DNA. I was a
professor at California State University, Sacramento from 1996-2023, where I developed and ran
an undergraduate education, research, and training program in forensic biology. I was the
DNA/biology advisor for the University of California, Davis Forensic Science Graduate Program
for five years, and have taught for the California Criminalistics Institute, the training arm of the
California Department of Justice Bureau of Forensic Services. I also give presentations
nationwide about forensic DNA evidence and its interpretation.

I’ve reviewed DNA discovery in over 200 criminal and civil cases, providing an independent
assessment of the evidence and serving as an educator for attorneys, judges, and juries. I
produced reports or testified in court in most of these cases and I stay current in the technologies
utilized by the profession. I view consulting as an extension of my teaching: translating complex
scientific ideas/concepts into clear, accessible language for non-experts.

My business office is in Oregon, but I consult with attorneys throughout the country and,
occasionally, overseas.

Chemistries and Instrumentation

ISPFS Crime Lab
   • Blood testing: presumptive ortho-tolidine
   • DNA extraction: EZ1 robot (elution volumes: 40-100 ul)DNA quantitation: Promega’s
      Plexor HY kit on a 7500 real-time PCR platform
   • DNA amplification: Promega’s PowerPlex Fusion
   • Capillary electrophoresis: ABI 3130 and 3500 Genetic Analyzers
   • Profile visualization and interpretation: Genemapper ID v3.2.1; AT 75 for all dye lanes
   • Probabilistic genotyping: STRmix v2.4.06 and v2.9.1
FBI Lab
   • Examination of hairs: stereomicroscopy and comparison microscopy
Bode Lab
   • Blood testing: presumptive phenolphthalein and human-specific Hematrace
   • DNA extraction: EZ1/EZ2 robot or manual (hair); elution volume 50 ul
   • DNA quantitation: Quantifiler Trio on a 7500 real-time PCR platform
   • DNA extract concentration: microcon
   • DNA amplification: Promega’s PowerPlex Fusion 6C
   • Capillary electrophoresis: ABI 3500 Genetic Analyzer
   • Profile visualization and interpretation: Genemapper ID-X v 1.6
   • Probabilistic genotyping: STRmix 2.5.11
Cybergenetics
   • TrueAllele® probabilistic genotyping software

Methodology

To arrive at my opinion, I reviewed the documents and DNA discovery listed below. I also
applied my extensive training in the forensic biology discipline, including my experience in the
laboratory using the chemistries and instrumentation utilized by the profession and my
experience performing forensic DNA case reviews nationwide. If I am asked to review additional
materials in the future, I reserve the right to change/update my opinion.

Rate

My rate for case reviews is $300.00 per hour. For testimony at deposition or trial, my rate is
$1,200.00 per half day or $2,000 per full day, with a minimum fee of $1,200 per day.

Case Background

The charges in this case are four counts of Capital Murder. The probable cause affidavit alleges
that four people in a single residence were killed by an edged weapon in the early morning hours
of November 13, 2022. Further review of pertinent police reports, video recordings, photographs
and investigative materials reveal that the State’s theory is that the perpetrator drove a vehicle to
the area of the home, parked, and 13 minutes later sped out of the neighborhood. This is
depicted on what is known to me as the 1112 King Road camera. 1

The house had three stories. The first floor (F1) included a west bedroom, an east bedroom, a
bathroom, and a furnace room. It was connected to the second flood (F2) by a stairway along the
north wall. The second floor (F2) included a living room, a bathroom, a west bedroom, an east
bedroom, a kitchen, and a storage room under the stairs. It was connected to the third floor (F3)
by a switchback staircase toward the south of the house. The third floor included a west
bedroom, a landing, a bathroom, and an east bedroom.

Decedents Mogen and Goncalves were located in the same bed on the third floor of the house
(F3 East Bedroom) while the other bedroom on that floor (F3 West Bedroom) was unoccupied.
When law enforcement arrived on the crime scene, Decedent Goncalves’ dog, Murphy, was on
the bed in this otherwise unoccupied room. Based upon my review of videos from the body worn
cameras from the first two officers on scene, I am aware that the bedroom doors to both
bedrooms were open.

Two roommates, Dylan Mortenson (occupant of F2 East Bedroom) and Bethany Funke
(occupant of F1 East Bedroom) were unharmed. The home had one other bedroom on the first
floor which was unoccupied (F1 West Bedroom).




1
 I am aware the allegation is that the vehicle made multiple passes before stopping for the 13 minutes depicted in
the camera.

                                                      003120
The bodies of Decedents Mogen and Goncalves were found in their shared bed in the F3 East
Bedroom. They both had extensive stab wounds. Decedent Goncalves also had extensive blunt
force trauma to her head and face. Each had minimal defensive wounds.

Decedent Kernodle was found on the floor of her bedroom (F2 West Bedroom). She had
approximately fifty (50) stab wounds, including to her face and head, and extensive defensive
wounds. Decedent Chapin’s body was located on the bed in the room. He had a deep stab wound
in his neck and large slash wounds elsewhere. Reference DNA samples were collected from
various potential suspects and persons of interest for comparison to DNA profiles obtained from
evidence.

On 12/30/2022, Bryan Kohberger, a graduate student living in the nearby town of Pullman,
Washington, was arrested. He was arrested in Pennsylvania where he was visiting his parents for
the holidays.

Evidence Collection and Testing

The attached spreadsheet, Serology and DNA Tests and Results, State v Bryan Kohberger, details
the very extensive list of evidence collected by police/crime scene investigators and the tests for
body fluids (serology) and/or DNA at the Crime Labs/companies involved in the analyses
(ISPFS Lab, FBI Lab, Bode Lab, and Cybergenetics).

I have summarized the information below, organized by collection location. Where possible, I
have listed the evidence collected in each location numerically by item number, in ascending
order, to keep things simple and easy to follow. The order of the items, as presented here, in no
way implies the importance or probative value of any single item of evidence in the case.

Crime Scene: 1122 King Road, Moscow ID

F3 East bedroom (Decedents Mogen’s bedroom but where she and Goncalves were located)

ISPFS Lab Item 1: Tan leather KA-BAR knife sheath; USMC with logo and snap button strap on
front (side A), belt loop, and sleeve (with rivets). Found on the bed beside the body of Decedent
Mogen and collected and sent to the ISPFS Crime Lab for swabbing and testing.
    • 1.1: One swab (taken at the Crime Lab) that was collected from the front strap snap
        closure area. An equivalent of 1,400 human cells’ worth of human DNA was recovered.
        A single source male profile was developed from the swab, and it matched the profile of
        the Mr. Kohberger. The DNA profile is at least 5.37 octillion times more likely if Mr.
        Kohberger is the source than if an unknown person is the source.
    • 1.2: One swab (taken at the Crime Lab) from the edges on the handle portion avoiding
        red-brown stains. Trace DNA and a partial DNA profile with at least three contributors
        including at least one male was recovered from the swab. Due to low level results and
        limited data in the profile, no comparisons could be made.
    • 1.3: One swab (taken at the Crime Lab) of the edges of the blade portion of the sheath.
        Trace DNA and a partial DNA profile with at least two contributors including at least one

Opinion

During the commission of a crime, cells, hair, and their DNA can be transferred from the
perpetrator to the victim, the victim to the perpetrator, the perpetrator to the crime scene
or a weapon, and from the victim to the crime scene or a weapon. This transfer can often


Page 17 of 20


                                              003133
be detected using forensic human DNA profiling techniques, and the information can
sometimes be very helpful in solving crimes.

The best sources of DNA in forensic investigations are hair, blood, semen, and cells from
the inside of body orifices (mouth, vagina, or rectum). At violent homicides, there is usually
copious DNA from the injured victims (due to bleeding) and sometimes from the
perpetrator (who may get injured during the attack). Being a liquid, blood spreads rapidly
and easily, soaking into clothing, footwear, bedding, carpet, and other items, and spattering
on walls, floors, people, weapons, and objects. Even if a perpetrator does not get injured
and does not leave his own blood behind, it is very difficult for him to leave the scene
without taking the blood of his victims with him. This is especially true when the attack is
“up close and personal,” like a knife killing, where there is direct contact between the
perpetrator and his victim(s). It is also especially true when there is limited time for a
perpetrator to “clean up” before leaving the scene.

It is also possible for a perpetrator to shed hair during a violent attack or pick up hairs
from the victim(s). Humans passively shed 50-100 hairs per day. They accumulate in our
homes and workplaces, and they adhere easily to clothing and other items. They may also
be actively pulled from the head during a violent altercation, either as the attacker
attempts to subdue the victim(s) or as the victims defend themselves and fight back. This is
one of the reasons why the hands of homicide victims are “bagged” before their bodies are
transported for autopsy. Hair pulled out by the roots can be an excellent source of DNA.

Surface skin cells are also a potential source of DNA, but because they are dead and no
longer contain a nucleus, their DNA is limited and is typically transferred at much lower
levels. Still, humans passively shed upward of 500 million skin cells per day, and modern
crime labs are equipped with highly sensitive instruments, chemistries, and computer
programs for detecting “trace DNA” and identifying its source.

The transfer of skin cell DNA is more difficult to contextualize than blood DNA transfer,
especially if it is found on small, portable items (e.g., ball caps, cell phones, cigarettes). The
question of how and why DNA transfers to an object, sometimes characterized as direct or
indirect transfer, is the subject of extensive research in the forensic community. Based on
this research, we know that people differ in the amount of DNA they shed into their
environment on any given day. A person can innocuously shed skin cells/DNA on the sides
of an item (e.g. a water bottle) and the item can be picked up and transported to a crime
scene by someone else who sheds no DNA onto it (either because they are wearing gloves or
because they are not shedding much DNA at the time). Skin cells are not like blood; we
shed them all day long during routine living and their presence does not suggest violence.
Thus, their detection on crime scene evidence must be viewed with caution, keeping in
mind innocent explanations.

Finally, there is no means to determine the age of DNA or of a particular deposit of
biological material. Even the presence of high-quality DNA is not an indicator that it was
shed recently.



Page 18 of 20


                                              003134
With these facts in mind, it’s my opinion that the biological/DNA evidence in the current
matter, State v Bryan Kohberger, paints a puzzling picture with limited support for the
State’s theory as well as evidence undermining that theory.

On the one hand:
   • There is good support that Mr. Kohberger’s DNA was found on Item 1.1, a swab
       from the knife sheath found beside Decedent Mogen’s body.
   • The sheath is designed to carry a knife consistent with injuries inflicted on the
       victims based on my review of the Latah County Prosecuting Attorney’s interview
       with Dr. Venna Singh, who performed the Decedents’ autopsies.

On the other hand:
   • Despite the large number of evidence items collected and tested, and the speed with
      which the bloody attacks purportedly took place, no blood, hair, or DNA from the
      victims was detected in Mr. Kohberger’s white Hyundai Elantra, his apartment, or
      his parents’ residence.
   • No blood, hair, or DNA from him was found on any of the crime scene evidence
      (except the touch DNA on the knife sheath).
   • No DNA or hair from him was found on any of the victims, including Decedent
      Kernodle who had extensive defensive wounds and clearly fought for her life.
   • DNA from an unknown male was detected on the left-hand fingernail clippings of
      Decedent Mogen. Cybergenetics excluded Mr. Kohberger as its source.
   • DNA from another unknown male (“Male B”) was found on a handrail at the crime
      scene, but the profile was never searched in CODIS, the national DNA database,
      and the police never investigated the lead further. Mr. Kohberger was excluded as
      the source of this DNA profile.
   • DNA from a third unknown male (“Male D”) was recovered from a glove found in
      the driveway at the crime scene. This profile was similarly never searched against
      CODIS or investigated further by police. Mr. Kohberger was excluded as the source
      of this DNA profile.
   • The knife pairing with the sheath was never found, so it cannot be tested for Mr.
      Kohberger’s DNA and the victims’ blood directly.
   • Moreover, the knife sheath is a moveable item, and while the DNA evidence suggests
      that Mr. Kohberger may have handled it at one time, it could have been brought to
      the crime scene by someone else.
   • Based on the lab reports and email correspondence between the ISPFS lab
      personnel and law enforcement, Mr. Kohberger’s DNA was detected on a swab
      taken from an area of the sheath that included the region underneath the cap
      portion of the snap (not on the top, exposed area of the cap, which was used for
      latent print analysis). This is a protected area where a prior handler’s DNA might
      be expected to persist even if the sheath was more recently held/used by someone
      else.
   • The DNA, by itself, contains no information on when it was deposited on the sheath,
      and it certainly does not place Mr. Kohberger at the crime scene with a knife in his
      hand when the victims were killed. Mr. Kohberger could have shed cells/DNA onto
      the sheath days, weeks, or even months earlier.

Page 19 of 20


                                           003135
I base this opinion on my education, years of experience and standard knowledge about
DNA transfer and the persistence of DNA on objects.

Overview

I am a human molecular geneticist with an expertise in forensic serology and DNA. I’ve been a
professor at California State University, Sacramento since 1998, where I developed and run an
undergraduate education, research, and training program in forensic biology. I was the
DNA/biology advisor for the University of California, Davis Forensic Science Graduate Program
for five years, and have taught for the California Criminalistics Institute, the training arm of the
California Department of Justice Bureau of Forensic Services.

I’ve reviewed DNA discovery in over 200 criminal and civil cases, providing an independent
assessment of DNA discovery and serving as an educator for attorneys, judges, and juries. I
produced reports or testified in court in most of these cases and I stay current in the technologies
utilized by the profession. I view consulting as an extension of my teaching: translating complex
scientific ideas/concepts into clear, accessible language for non-experts.

My business office is in Oregon, but I consult with attorneys throughout the country and,
occasionally, overseas.

A.      INTRODUCTION

On November 13, 2022, after about 4 am, Ethan Chapin, Xana Kernodle, Kaylee Goncalves, Madison
Mogen had a home invasion at 1122 King Road, Moscow, Idaho. After a 911 phone call at about 11:58 am,
police found four victims. Chapin, Kernodle, Goncalves, and Mogen were deceased with edged weapon
wounds. The Police arrested Bryan Kohberger based in part due to the Police investigation of video
surveillance camera footage of an unknown vehicle
a white 2015 Hyundai Elantra sedan.

The purpose of my investigation is to analyze the various surveillance videos and to determine if the Police
analysis of the video data was proper and consistent with determining that the make and model of an



My investigation into this matter and the preparation of this report were performed at the request of the
appointed counsel on behalf of Mr. Kohberger.

This report is based on information currently available to me. I reserve the right to amend or supplement
my analysis in this report and/or to respond to any additional submissions prepared by or on behalf of the
parties. I also reserve the right to amend or supplement my opinions based on further discovery and
information provided in the case. I reserve the right to create any additional summaries, tutorials,
demonstrations, charts, drawings, tables and/or animations that may be appropriate to supplement and
demonstrate my opinions, as necessary. All the opinions stated in this report are based on my own
personal knowledge and professional judgment and are to a degree of reasonable scientific certainty.

I received a Bachelor of Science degree in Mechanical Engineering (with Aerospace) from the Worcester
Polytechnic Institute, Worcester, Massachusetts, in 1992. I received a Master of Business Administration
from Syracuse University, Syracuse, New York in 2007. I have certificates in crash reconstruction from
Northwestern University and other sources. Presently, I am employed by Robson Forensic, located in
Lancaster, Pennsylvania and provide technical investigations, analysis, reports, and testimony in litigation
involving, for example, product liability, accident reconstruction, intellectual property, mechanical
engineering, and photogrammetric/video analysis. I also perform engineering and testing consulting for
non-litigation clients.

I am a member of the Society of Automotive Engineers and have published several articles with them (as
listed in my CV). I am a certified Pennsylvania motor vehicle safety inspector. I am trained in crash
reconstruction with certificates from Northwestern University Center for Public Safety. While at Magna
Powertrain I managed a fleet of over 100 vehicles for their maintenance and over the road and off-road
collision investigation. While at Chrysler I was test engineer responsible for conducting testing on
numerous varieties of vehicles. Since college I have been using video and imagery as a sensor for object
detection and making measurements. At Magna I developed vision systems for detecting and counting
bolts on an assembly using cameras. We utilized cameras in test cells for durability, end-of-line validation
testing, and over-the-road vehicle testing.

Officer Payne reported that:
On November 13, 2022, at about 4 pm he responded to 1122 King Road, Moscow, Idaho and found officers
processing the scene that included the bodies of Chapin, Kernodle, Goncalves, and Mogen. There were
two witnesses in the residence that stated everyone was home by 2 am, and there was DoorDash delivery

the incident occurred at 4 to 4:25 am and thus collected neighboring video evidence from that timeframe.
Based on video evidence Payne
    1. Westbound near 700 Indian Hills Drive at 3:26 am
    2. Westbound near the intersection of Styner Avenue and Highway 95 at 3:28 am. (a lack of front
         license plate is identified)
    3. Making 4 passes near 1122 King Road and Walenta Drive from 3:29 to 4:20 am. (with a few other
         vehicles driving in the area)
    4. Eastbound on King Road at 4:04
    5. Turning around at 500 Queen Road #52
    6. Westbound on King Road attempting to park or turn around in front of 1112 King Road.
    7. Making a three-point turn at the intersection of Queen and King, to drive eastbound on Queen.
    8. Departing near 1112 King Road at about 4:20 am. Driving away on Palouse River Drive and
         Conestoga Drive.
    9. An FBI forensic examiner found a video to show white 2011 to 2016 Hyundai Elantra.

E.       ANALYSIS


Digital video is a series of digital images (frames). Image resolution is how many pixels (digital points of
color) vertical and horizontal are used to create the image. More pixels in an image provide greater detail
of the objects in the image. The various video files have different resolutions, camera lens types (degrees
on convex lens), external lighting, coloration (black and white, full color, night vision infrared), frame rate,
and vantage distance to the vehicle of interest. Same sized objects that are closer to the camera will
occupy a greater number of pixels than objects farther away from the camera. Color is stored.

The Police generated a digital map image showing the locations of the cameras and their expected path
of a vehicle of interest (Video file Sequence 01           -

Photogrammetry is the science associated with determining measurement and the size of objects in digital
images. The Scientific Working Group on Digital Evidence (SWGDE) best practices includes a description
of photogrammetric measurements1 and is composed of members from government, law enforcement,
private industry, and academia involved in the digital and multimedia forensic profession.




                               Image 21 The 2015 Hyundai Elantra dimensions

Photogrammetric measurements were not reported to have been performed by the Police to determine
                                         Without a size and shape overlay comparison or in video
measurements the Police did not distinguish between the models of vehicles that have consistent size in
the videos from near the incident scene. There is no evidence that the Police presented that shows other
models of vehicles did not have similar features to the unknown suspect vehicle or unknown vehicles of
interest (for example one popular model sedan, the Honda Accord does not have the body lines similar to
the unknown suspect vehicle and can be ruled out as not similar). The Police only provided confirmation
bias, by using a known target vehicle model, and matching characteristics instead of eliminating all other
potential similar vehicles that contain these characteristics (otherwise they would have included the
Sonata and Legacy). This fails to meet reasonable scientific certainty from their analysis. The Police
analysis and determination of the make and model of the unknown suspect vehicles was improper and
lacked other possible vehicle models with similar characteristics.

There was no paint transfer or physical evidence to confirm the
color. Based on the video images the paint color may be white, silver, or another light color as the videos
were taken at night and each camera in the area of the incident had a different hue for the vehicle (color
tinting bias). Additionally, as the videos have demonstrated, it is not determinable if these videos all
contain the same unknown vehicle.

have a visible front license plate also do not have a visible rear license plate, as the operator may have

this piece of information does not result in the conclusion that the unknown suspect vehicle or this vehicle
on S. Main Street were from Pennsylvania. The Police opinion about the unknown subject vehicle not
having a license plate at the incident is improper.

Lastly, there were about 1.3 million Hyundai Elantra sold in the United States between 2011 and 2016,2.
There was a total of about 43 million passenger cars sold in that same time period,3 and of those white is
the most popular color with about 25%, gray and silver also being light colors and the next most popular
colors with another about 30% combined.4 So, there is a pool of a possible about 650,000 light-colored
Elantra vehicles and possibly more that could match the unknown suspect vehicle that was in the area of
the incident, that the Police did not investigate. Narrowing by registrations geographically could not
eliminate vehicles from the potential pool of owners, as there are two universities in the area that draw
people from around the country.

5-12 and 15-16) on roadways that had access to the incident site and no other exit and entrance roads.

F.       FINDINGS

Within a reasonable degree of professional and scientific certainty and subject to change if additional
information becomes available, it is my opinion that:

     1. Most of the videos relied upon by the Police do not contain sufficient detail to determine
        the unknown subject vehicle make or model.
     2. From the current evidence various unknown suspect vehicles are not identifiable as a
        specific make and model based on the Indian Hills Drive, Linda Lane, King Road, Paradise
        Drive videos.
     3. The only videos from a location near the area of incident and generally near the time of
        the incident that can allow for a determination of an unknown suspect vehicle make and
        model were the 1125 Ridge Road videos. These videos show that it was likely a Hyundai
        Elantra, and shares many characteristics with a Sonata, or Subaru Legacy.
     4. The Police analysis and determination of the make and model of the unknown suspect
        vehicles was improper and lacked other possible vehicle models with similar
        characteristics.
     5. Several hours after the incident at about 9 am a vehicle consistent with a white 2015
        Hyundai was on S Main Street.
     6. The Police opinion about the unknown subject vehicle not having a license plate at around
        the time of the incident is improper.
     7. There was video evidence from the area on 11/13/22, between 0200 and 0500 hours, that
        shows vehicles that have vehicle characteristics that are similar in shape and geometry to
        the identifiable characteristics from the King Road and Linda Lane video images.

#1  Basis for My Opinion: High-quality photographs or scans of all fingerprint evidence
in the case were requested. Scans should be made at a minimum resolution of 1000
pixels per inch (PPI) and saved in a non-proprietary, non-destructive format such as TIF
(no compression). Images should be individually scanned and NOT submitted in multi-
page formats.

If the item was only photographed or scanned, as was the case for latent impressions
developed with dye stains or chemical processes, then copies of the original digital image
files should be submitted. Any enhanced images used for comparison should also be
included.

Photocopies of fingerprints or scans saved in PDF format are NOT acceptable for
comparison purposes. Many crime labs and law enforcement agencies provide attorneys
with copies of their reports, which may include images of the impression evidence, in PDF
format. While these images may be acceptable for demonstrative purposes, they are
NOT acceptable for forensi¢ analysis or comparison.

It must be noted that all applications used to create PDF documents not only resample
the image (reducing the number of pixels in the image) but also compress the image using
JPG compression. Some PDF creator applications, such as Adobe Acrobat Pro, allow
you to control both the resolution and JPG compression level, as shown below. Image


                                            5




                                            003198
quality can be further degraded if the PDF document is printed using a laser or inkjet
printer.

Again, forensic evidentiary images embedded in PDF documents do not provide sufficient
image quality, rendering them unsuitable for examination, analysis, or comparison.

Idaho State Police Forensic Latent Print Examination Report (10 Report M2022-4843)
states, "Latent Prints L1 do not contain a sufficient amount of clear ridge detail necessary
for comparison."

#2 My Examination/Opinion: conducted my own independent examination of the digital
                                               |




images received of Latent Prints L1 (items # 32.1 through 32.3) and concur with the
                                                                                        6




                                                                                        003199
conclusions of the Idaho State Police Forensic Services. Latent Print L1 does not contain
sufficient, clear ridge detail necessary for comparison.

#2 Basis for My Opinion: The accepted methodology of fingerprint examination is
referred to as "ACE-V" (pronounced "Ace Vee"). An examination begins with "A," the
analysis of one fingerprint without regard to any other fingerprints. A fingerprint may be
analyzed for anatomical inferences (which area of a finger or hand), matrix (observations
regarding the transfer medium or material that was transferred in the touch, e.g., sweat,
ink, etc.), substrate (the surface on which the fingerprint was deposited), development
medium (chemicals or powders used to make the print visible), distortion, pressure, angle
of touch, slippage, normal handling considerations, the direction the finger was pointing,
etc. The "A" or analysis of a fingerprint is an information-gathering process in which
careful observation informs the examiner of a multitude of facts about the fingerprint.

In the analysis phase of the examination, the examiner also considers fingerprint features
or characteristics classified as Level 1, Level 2, or Level 3 detail based on physical
dimension and their correspondence with other ridges and details in proximity to the detail
being compared. In general, "Level 1" refers to the overall pattern of a fingerprint (loop,
arch, or whorl), which is the tendency of the ridges to flow in concert with each other.
"Level 2" refers, in part, to the features commonly referred to as "points," such as ending
ridges (ridge endings), splitting ridges (bifurcations), and dots (single ridge units not
connected to an adjacent ridge). Level 3 refers to finer, often microscopic detail, contained
within a single ridge and not reflected by a deviation in the ridge path of adjacent ridges.
For example, sweat pores and small bumps on the edge of a ridge are considered Level
3 details.


The combination of quality and quantity of detail is also considered in the analysis phase.
Some fingerprints have sufficient quality (clarity) and quantity of detail to affect an
identification (identification or exclusion / no identification, provided another fingerprint of
sufficient quality is available for comparison.) Some fingerprints may have sufficient
quality and quantity of detail to exclude a print as coming from the same source, but do
not contain sufficient detail to make a positive identification. Some fingerprints lack
sufficient quality and quantity of detail to identify or exclude the impression, and are
considered to be of no value for comparison. This was the conclusion determined for
Latent Print L1.

                                               003200
                                             KKK




#3 Agency Examination: Items # 32.4 through 32.6: digital copies of purported latent
print lift L2 from "EXT Lower Pane of South Kitchen Window."

Idaho State Police Forensic Field Services Report (22-M09903 #11) states, "powder
processed the following areas: the exterior lower pane of the south kitchen window..."
"latent lift cards (latents L2 ...) were collected from the exterior lower pane of the south
kitchen window."

Idaho State Police Forensic Latent Print Examination Report (10 Report M2022-4843)
states, "Latent Prints L2 do not contain a sufficient amount of clear ridge detail necessary
for comparison."

#3 My Examination/Opinion: conducted my own independent examination of the digital
                                |




images received of Latent Prints L2 (items # 32.4 through 32.6) and do not concur with
the conclusions of the Idaho State Police Forensic Services. In my opinion, Latent Prints
L2 do contain a sufficient amount of clear ridge detail necessary for comparison.

|
 compared Latent Prints L2 to digital copies of friction ridge exemplars bearing the names
of Bryan Kohberger, Ethan Chapin, Kaylee Goncalves, Xana Kernodle, Madison Mogen,
Dylan Mortensen, Bethany Funke, Emily Alandt, Connor Chesnut, Hunter Johnson, and
John Showalter.

No Identifications were made to any of the digital copies of friction ridge exemplars of the
above individuals, including the defendant, Bryan Kohberger.

#3 Basis for My Opinion: Because friction ridges are unique and persistent, they can
leave prints that record the details in the skin that can be compared and determined to
have been left by the same area of friction ridge skin. The latent print and exemplar prints
are compared by examining the preserved friction ridge skin details at three levels. First,
the overall ridge flow or pattern of the ridges are compared to determine if similar patterns
are present in both the latent print and any area of the exemplars.

Next, individual ridge details are compared, looking for corresponding (matching) ridge
endings, splitting ridges, and dots. These splitting ridges, ending ridges, and dots are
sometimes referred to as "points."

Finally, the degree to which the actual configuration of sweat pores and surrounding
tissue of the individual eccrine glands (ridge units) is distinct may also be compared
between the two prints.




                                              8




                                              003201
If the latent print and the exemplar (known print) were made by the same area of friction
ridge skin, there should be agreement (continuity and consistency) of all three levels of
detail visible in both prints. If there is a sufficient quantity of features in the same relative
positions with no features exhibiting a discrepancy, then a latent print examiner trained to
competency can conclude that both prints must have been made by the same area of
friction ridge skin. That is the point at which the examiner claims an "identification."

The inability to make any determination of identification or no identification may be due to
inadequate quality or quantity of detail in one or both prints. In some comparisons, it is
not possible to reach any conclusion regarding either identification or no identification due
to inadequate quality and quantity of detail in either the latent print or the exemplar (known
print), and the examination is referred to as "inconclusive."

#6 Agency Examination: Latent # L3: purported digital impression from "2"¢ Floor West
Bedroom Window."

#6 My Examination/Opinion:         conducted my own independent examination of the
                                    |




digital images received of Latent # L3 and concur with the conclusion of the Idaho State
Police Forensic Latent Print Analysis Notes. The impression is consistent with that of a
possible fabric impression, and no impressions of friction ridges were observed.

#6 Basis for My Opinion: Fabric impressions can result when fabric comes in contact
with a surface capable of retaining the pattern. A fabric impression can contain

                                            10



                                            003203
characteristics such as weave and whether the fabric has unique features such as tears,
wrinkles, creases, or wear patterns. However, as they are not impressions left by the
ridges and furrows found on friction ridge skin, they cannot be compared and attributed
to individuals like fingerprints can be.




#7 Agency Examination: Latent # L4: purported digital impression from "2°? Floor East
Bedroom Threshold."

Idaho State Police Forensic Latent Print Analysis Notes (22-W09903 #5) state Latent Print
"L4 is a possible shoe impression" that was not analyzed.

#7 My Examination/Opinion: conducted my own independent examination of the digital
                                |




images received of Latent # L4 and concurred with the conclusion of the Idaho State
Police Forensic Latent Print Analysis Notes. The impression is consistent with that of a
possible shoe impression and no impressions of friction ridge detail were observed.

#7 Basis for My Opinion: A footwear impression is typically formed when the outsole of
a shoe is contaminated with some foreign matter such as dirt, dust, blood, moisture, etc.,
and comes in contact with a surface, such as a floor, threshold, wall, and so on.

In some instances, features may be present in the footwear impressions, such as
footwear outsole patterns (herringbone pattern, wave pattern, etc.), specific outsole
design (design elements of a footwear outsole), or randomly acquired characteristics
(such as cuts, scratches, tears, holes, abrasions and/or the acquisition of debris). In some
instances, these features can have a [latent] "impression-like" appearance caused by
distortion, improper recovery methods, photographic issues, etc.

In this case, the partial features were not left by ridges and furrows found on friction ridge
skin, so they could not be analyzed or compared as fingerprints.

#13 My Examination/Opinion: From my observations of the first officer walking through
and securing the scene, followed by subsequent officers, it appears many areas that were
overlooked and/or potentially damaged/contaminated for potential processing for latent
prints.

| made observations of potential areas for detection, preservation and/or processing
impression evidence. The list is not all conclusive, having come from video observations
only.

             walls up the staircase. Officers were observed in the video touching these
             areas as they proceeded up the stairs. Latent impressions can be very
             fragile and can be easily damaged or removed.

              the kitchen slider door.

Based on my own years of training and experience regarding the processing of crime
scenes, especially in the cases of murder, all sinks in the kitchen and bathrooms should
be checked for the possibility of latents due to washing up, etc. Doors, door knobs, door
frames and walls entering all rooms, including all bathrooms should be checked for the
possibility of latent prints. Toilet seats and covers in the bathrooms should be checked
for latent prints. Items, including towels in bathrooms/kitchen should be examined for
blood stains, etc.

Legs of tables and chairs in rooms where the murders occurred should be examined
and processed for latent prints, blood, etc.

#13 Basis for My Opinion: "Of all major crimes, homicide investigation requires the
greatest effort on the part of the police. The investigator is responsible for collecting a
vast amount of evidence and coordinating information from various sources such as
witnesses, the suspect, the officers involved with the crime scene, the forensic
pathologist, and the criminalist. Death investigation requires a team effort, and only
through cooperation of persons from many disciplines, coordination of efforts, and
extreme attention to detail can a successful conclusion of an investigation be realized."
(Techniques of Crime Scene Investigation; 4" Edition; by Barry A.J. Fisher, Arne
Svensson, and Otto Wendel")
                                             17




                                             003210
"Once the investigation has begun, even items that may seem unimportant and of no
value should be considered as potential evidence. In a murder investigation, there is
usually an abundance of evidence, even in those cases where the suspect attempted to
clean up after the crime. Even in the so-called "perfect murder," there will be much
evidence to aid in the crime's solution. There is, in fact, no perfect murder only cases
                                                                           -




where there is a failure to prove a deliberate killing." (Techniques of Crime Scene
Investigation; 4th Edition; by Barry A.J. Fisher, Arne Svensson, and Otto Wendel').

                              DANIEL HELLWIG

Daniel Hellwig, Forensic Director, Intermountain Forensics, may testify for the

defense as an expert regarding SNP and WGS testing, bioinformatics, lab protocols

and implementation of IGG standards in the forensic community.                  Hellwig’s

opinion/testimony will be based on his experience, education, and trainings as

detailed in his curriculum vitae which is included with this response as Exhibit D4-B.

       It is anticipated that Daniel Hellwig’s testimony in trial will be consistent

with his testimony at the Motion to Suppress hearing. A formal report will be

forthcoming and disclosed to the State upon receipt.

 It is anticipated that Dr. Hellwig will testify in the following areas:

           a. The efforts of the forensic community to implement standards in for
              IGG consistent with forensic laboratories and why such standards are
              necessary to ensure that testing is conducted in a reliable, reproducible
              manner. This testimony will encompass

                  i. the requirement to create and retain technical records

                  ii. the requirement to provide written or electronic reports

                 iii. the validation of methods used, including computer programs

                 iv. the development of protocols that lay out methods used as well
                     as quality control/quality assurance standards

                  v. the need for documentation of quality standards such as
                     contamination logs, corrective actions and root cause analysis of
                     laboratory errors

                 vi. the technical review of case documentation and reports

                vii. proficiency testing of individuals involved in case work

                viii. the retention of documentation including methods used and
                      digital data files

           b. How SNP testing is conducted by commercial labs such as Othram,
              what types of material and documentation is typically generated by a
                                            2

                                         003219
                    lab conducting such testing, including digital data files.
                 c. The type of information that can be obtained from a SNP or WGS data
                    set, in particular personal medical information and how the test results
                    differ from standard STR testing.

                 d. How bioinformatic programs operate in general on the raw data
                    generated by the SNP testing process and how these programs are used
                    to generate data that can be uploaded to commercial databases.

                 e. The need to maintain laboratory documentation including protocols
                    and data files and the reason for such documentation and retention.

                 f. The importance of external review of forensic testing in general and
                    IGG specifically

                 g. The use of commercial databases in building out family trees used to
                    identify an unknown individual from a crime scene sample. This
                    testimony will encompass:

                 h. The types of databases available and how they are used in an IGG
                    investigation

                 i. The limits on the use of these databases and the privacy concerns that
                    form the basis of these limits and the development of the opt in/opt out
                    functions for law enforcement access and how they work

                 j. The history of the abuse of these databases leading to the restriction of
                    law enforcement use of various databases


       This disclosure is provided as a summary. Further detail about the scope and breadth of his

testimony may be found in his report and his curriculum vitae. Mr. Hellwig may offer testimony to

refute any expert opinion not yet disclosed by the State.

Leah Larkin, PhD
I have an undergraduate degree in Biology from Swarthmore College in Pennsylvania and
a PhD in Botany from the University of Texas at Austin. My graduate and postdoctoral
work included analyzing DNA data to understand how species are related to one another.
I have been doing genetic genealogy since 2013 and doing it professionally since 2016.
In that time, I have resolved hundreds of unknown parent, grandparent, or great
grandparent cases and spearheaded a more scientific approach to autosomal DNA
analysis, including co-developing computational tools for evaluating relationships.



Genetic Genealogy Searching
Genetic genealogy combines traditional genealogical research using historical records
with the analysis of DNA data from direct-to-consumer testing companies. This approach
can often answer genealogical questions that cannot be resolved with documents alone.
Examples include identifying an unknown biological parent, grandparent, or more distant
ancestor. It can also be used to identify DNA samples of unknown origin, including but
not limited to DNA found at crime scenes.

Genetic genealogy and its forensic counterpart (variously called forensic or investigative
genetic genealogy and abbreviated FGG, FIGG, or IGG) typically uses autosomal DNA
(atDNA), which makes up roughly 95% of our genomes and accounts for the majority of
our heritable physical, psychological, and health traits. Autosomal DNA is inherited
equally from both parents and can be used to investigate both the maternal and paternal
branches of a person’s family.1 The testing companies typically provide estimates of the
geographic regions that contributed to the tester’s genetic makeup (sometimes called
ethnicity estimates) as well as a list of "DNA matches" who share atDNA with the tester.
Each company has its own proprietary algorithms for these reports.

Generally speaking, the more atDNA two people share in centimorgans (cM), the more
closely related they are.2 However, the correlation is not exact. For example, someone

1
  For genealogical use, there are three categories of DNA based on the inheritance pattern: Y-chromosome DNA
(Y-DNA; inherited from fathers to sons), mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA; inherited from mothers to children), and
autosomal DNA (inherited from both parents to children). Y-DNA and mtDNA are only useful for tracing the direct
paternal and maternal lineages, respectively. Because atDNA is inherited from both parents and all four
grandparents, it can be used to investigate all branches of a person’s family tree.
2
  A centimorgan (cM) is a measure of genetic distance between two points on a DNA chromosome. During egg and
sperm production, a biological process called “crossing over” occurs. By definition, a 100-cM segment of DNA




                                                    003230
who shares 100 cM could be anywhere from a half 1st cousin to a 5th cousin. The
genealogist must use genealogical records, statistical analysis, knowledge of the source
populations, and logical inference to determine the true relationship.

In the 2010s, amateur genealogists developed strategies to help people identify unknown
biological family, for example, the parents of an adoptee. The genetic genealogist first
builds family pedigrees for the top DNA matches to find their relationships to one
another.3 If two matches share great grandparents and match the adoptee in the 2nd cousin
range, the genealogist might pursue other descendants of that ancestral couple to find
possible candidates for the adoptee’s biological parent. However, given the variability in
DNA sharing, the connection could be one or two generations further back.

The search can be narrowed by tying in matches on other family lines. For example, if the
suspected great grandparents had eight children, one cannot initially tell which of the
eight was the direct ancestor of the adoptee. However, if there is a reasonable DNA
match who is related to the spouse of one of those children, the genealogist might assume
that the adoptee is descended from that child (and their spouse) rather than from one of
the other seven siblings.

Descendancy research is an iterative process, where the focus is refined by repeatedly
adding new matches to the analysis. When informative matches are not available, the
genealogist might use another DNA database or might reach out to potential relatives and
ask them to do a DNA test. The goal is to find closer DNA matches that might narrow the
focus of the search. A research tree in such a case typically includes hundreds or
thousands of people before the parents are identified.

Another complicating factor is that some groups tend to marry within themselves, whether
for religious, cultural, or geographic reasons. This practice is called endogamy. For
genetic genealogy (including FGG), atDNA can be difficult to analyze in endogamous
groups, because individuals are often related several times over and share more DNA than
might be expected based on the closest relationship. The amount of endogamy varies by
group, as does the impact it has on DNA matching. Some common endogamous groups
in the US are Ashkenazi Jews, Hispanics, Cajuns, and Italians.

The methods developed by amateur genealogists can also be used to identify DNA from a
crime scene. Ideally, the DNA matches will point to both parents of the person of interest,
and the investigation can focus on the children of that couple. If the matches guide the
genealogist to only one set of potential grandparents or great grandparents, the scope of
the investigation is much broader. Dozens or hundreds of innocent people can be
implicated in an FGG search, depending on how close the initial matches are.



will cross over once on average per generation. Crossing over causes shared DNA segments to decrease in size over
generational time.

The main differences in methodology between an adoptee search and an FGG search are
how the DNA is sampled and analyzed and in which genealogy databases can be used.



DNA Analysis for Forensic Genetic Genealogy

The human genome is the “instruction manual” for the human body. It comprises more
than 3 billion nucleotide base pairs (chemical building blocks), each of which can take
one of four forms (A, C, G, or T). The sequence and order of those nucleotides provide
chemical instructions to build and maintain the body. The vast majority our nucleotides
are identical among all people, while a small fraction provides the instructions that make
each of us unique. Some so-called “junk DNA” has no known function.

The United States justice system has used junk DNA for identification since the 1990s.4
The 13–20 short DNA sequences (markers) used in the Combined DNA Index System
(CODIS) were chosen specifically to avoid trait information, like race, physical
appearance, or health information. In that respect, they work much like a fingerprint:
they help with identity only while avoiding private information that might be
constitutionally protected.

The DNA markers used for genetic genealogy are fundamentally different. Direct-to-
consumer genealogy companies use technology called a “DNA microarray” (a.k.a., “DNA
chip”) that analyzes roughly 700,000 bases known to vary among individuals. The
variable positions are called single nucleotide polymorphisms or SNPs (pronounced snips).

Microarrays were invented for biomedical research. The manufacturer of the DNA chip
most commonly used for genetic genealogy boasts its “Clinical research applications
include disease risk profiling studies, pharmacogenomics research, wellness
characterization, and complex disease discovery.”5 In addition to benign traits like
appearance and race, these tests can reveal genetic risks such as addiction, Alzheimer’s,
autism, bipolar disorder, cancer, cystic fibrosis, heart disease, schizophrenia, and many
more.6

Thus, unlike the CODIS markers, which were selected to avoid biomedical details,
microarrays intentionally target some of our most intensely private information.
Microarray use for genealogy was an afterthought.

For best results, microarrays require 100–200 ng of high quality, single-source DNA. That
is often not available from crime scenes, where the DNA sample may be low in quantity,

                                                    003232
degraded, contaminated with non-human DNA, and/or a mixture of two or more
individuals. An alternative approach for these samples is whole genome sequencing
(WGS, a.k.a., next generation sequencing or NGS). A WGS file has even more private
genetic information than a microarray file.

Once the WGS data file is obtained, it must be manipulated to make it compatible with
the genealogy databases. WGS files are too large for the databases, so extra data must be
stripped out to just the SNPs the genealogy companies use, and missing or ambiguous
data must be added using statistical methods. Adjustments might also be needed for
contaminants, like bacterial or fungal DNA. This process is called bioinformatics.

Bioinformatics can also be used on microarray results to add in data that was not
generated in the original analysis. One might do this to fill in gaps in the original data,
e.g., from poor-quality source DNA, or to match to kits from other DNA companies that
tested different SNPs using a different microarray chip.7 The “new” data is based on
statistical comparisons to the genomes of unrelated individuals in a reference set rather
than based on direct analysis of the forensic sample.

Once a suitable forensic DNA profile has been achieved, it is uploaded to one or more
genealogy databases to be matched to layperson genealogists. At this point, the FGG
search proceeds much like a regular genetic genealogy search, using genealogical records,
people-finder sites, newspapers, social media, etc. to infer relationships and track down
people. Investigative agencies will have access to resources that a layperson genealogist
does not.



Forensic Genetic Genealogy Databases

The arrest of the serial Golden State Killer on 24 April 2018, rocked the genealogy world,
because Joseph James DeAngelo was identified using genetic genealogy. In response to
public outcry over law enforcement agents searching DNA databases without user
consent, the three largest databases (AncestryDNA, 23andMe, and MyHeritage) all
explicitly forbade FGG. Meanwhile, two smaller databases, GEDmatch and
FamilyTreeDNA, chose to allow FGG investigations for violent crimes and unknown
human remains.

The systems at both GEDmatch and FamilyTreeDNA evolved over time in response to a
series of scandals and privacy breaches.8 After GEDmatch allowed genealogist CeCe
Moore to investigate a case that did not qualify for FGG under their Terms of Service, they

created an “opt in” system for FGG matching.9,10 All existing users were hidden from
forensic matching, and only those who explicitly consented (i.e., opted in) were to be
matched to forensic kits. However, it was an “open secret” in the FGG community that
forensic kits could access users who were opted out of FGG matching using “loopholes”
in GEDmatch’s programming.11 The loopholes were reportedly fixed in September 2023.

FamilyTreeDNA collaborated with the FBI on the Golden State Killer case with the explicit
stipulation that their involvement be kept from the public.12 In late 2018, they quietly
changed their Terms of Service to allow FGG cases but failed to notify their users as
required.13 In response to the backlash, they created an “opt out” system in which most
users were exposed to FGG matching by default (i.e., opted in) but could change their
settings to opt out.14 Because FamilyTreeDNA’s users are opted in by default, the vast
majority have not given affirmative consent for FGG matching.

Both FamilyTreeDNA and GEDmatch have designated, fee-based portals through which
forensic DNA profiles should be uploaded. The GEDmatch portal is called GEDmatch
Pro; the FamilyTreeDNA portal does not have a unique name to my knowledge. Once
uploaded through the portal, the forensic profile is matched to laypeople in the database
who are opted in to FGG matching but not to those who are opted out. Thus, a forensic
profile that has been properly uploaded can only access a subset of the entire database,
the portion that is opted in.

Because GEDmatch and FamilyTreeDNA have relatively small databases (I estimate 2
million and 1.7 million profiles, respectively), and because not all users are opted in to
FGG matching, law enforcement agents have an incentive to access more kits. As
outlined above, one way to do that was to use a security “loophole” at GEDmatch to
match to kits that were opted out. Another is to upload an FGG kit through the layperson
portals at GEDmatch and/or FamilyTreeDNA to avoid the restrictions, or to upload it to a
larger database like MyHeritage that explicitly forbids FGG matching.15 The Israeli

Department of Justice Interim Policy on Forensic Genetic Genealogy

As noted above, microarray and WGS profiles contains extremely private genetic
information that may be constitutionally protected. The US Supreme Court alluded to the
privacy implications of FGG in their 2013 decision in Maryland v King.

        “The CODIS loci come from noncoding parts of the DNA that do not reveal
        the genetic traits of the arrestee. While science can always progress further,
        and those progressions may have Fourth Amendment consequences, alleles
        at the CODIS loci ‘are not at present revealing information beyond
        identification.’”16 (Emphasis mine.)

Microarrays and WGS are precisely the type of scientific progression impacting significant
privacy rights that may have Fourth Amendment consequences. These tests can reveal
information that most Americans would consider to be intensely personal, like
extramarital sex, incest, racial/ethnic background, genetic diseases, and propensity for
psychiatric problems.

The U.S. Department of Justice acknowledged these privacy concerns in its 2019 interim
policy on FGG searching (FGGS). “The Department must use FGGS in a manner
consistent with the requirements and protections of the Constitution and other legal
authorities.”17 In addition to other stipulations, the DOJ policy requires that:

        “Investigative agencies shall identify themselves as law enforcement to GG
        services and enter and search FGG profiles only in those GG services that
        provide explicit notice to their service users and the public that law
        enforcement may use their service sites to investigate crimes or to identify
        unidentified human remains.”18

Only two genetic genealogy services of any consequence meet the DOJ criteria for
FGG: GEDmatch Pro and FamilyTreeDNA’s forensic portal.19

My Role

I was engaged by Mr. Kohberger’s legal defense team on 27 Jul 2023 to provide my expert
opinion on the FGG performed in this case. My ability to do that has been hampered by
an ongoing lack of disclosure regarding these materials. As of the date of this report, the
defense still has not received all of the materials necessary for me to do a full evaluation of
the FGG work.

Obtaining the underlying FGG documents via discovery has been an extremely involved
and drawn-out process. While some of the requested documents have been produced,
many others either have not been provided at all, or the defense has been prohibited by
court order from using them to full effect.

For example:

     1.   Othram either did not preserve its protocols, standard operating procedures,
          validation summaries, error logs, bench notes, and analytical data files as an
          accredited lab would, or, if it did, what it passed on to the FBI has not been
          produced.20 Even though Othram was under instruction to “preserve the whole
          genome profile that you have generated on this case, any remaining DNA extract (if
          existing), any data generated on this case, any other records they have on this case,
          and anything else laid out in the state contract with Idaho,” that work has never
          been shared with the defense.21

     2.   The FBI did not preserve its work in a way that allows me to evaluate their
          genealogical analysis. Typically, a genealogist builds a “research tree” using
          genealogical software; the contents of that tree can be exported as a “gedcom”
          file.22 In addition, genetic genealogists typically download and store a list of DNA
          matches from each matching database for preservation and for use offline. These
          files include the name or alias of each DNA match, an email address, the amount
          of shared DNA, the size of the longest shared DNA segment, and other
          information. If the FBI preserved these standard items, it did not disclose them to
          the defense.

     3.   The prosecution produced two SNP profiles, one labeled “Othram Profile” and one
          labeled “FBI SNP Profile.” These profiles are simple text files that can be opened in
          any text editor. A complete set of the underlying data for these two profiles has
          never been produced in this case. In fact, the defense has not been provided with
          protocols and procedures explaining what type of analysis was done to generate
          either data file. Othram advertises “Forensic Grade Genome Sequencing™,” but
          based on the size of their data file, they may have done a microarray rather than

The FBI Violated the Department of Justice Policy on FGG

In March 2024, I reviewed discovery materials that had been provided to me. Based on
that review, I was reasonably certain that the FBI had searched databases they were
forbidden to use. This was later confirmed to be true by the FBI. In so doing, they
violated the Department of Justice Interim Policy on FGG as well as the contractual Terms
of Service of the databases they searched.

Othram was contracted to produce a SNP profile from the crime scene sample, upload it
to approved genealogy databases, and perform genealogical research.25 They uploaded
the crime scene profile to FamilyTreeDNA and GEDmatch Pro, the two main databases
that allow forensic genetic genealogy searches (FGGS), on or before 8 December 2022. I
have no reason to believe that Othram did not follow the appropriate protocols to access
those two databases.

Othram was ordered to cease work on the case on 10 December 2022, and they prepared
a preliminary report six days later.26 Based on that report, the most informative matches

RK and HS are third cousins to one another and share a set of 2nd great grandparents, Clark

that the unknown subject was descended from one of the eight children of the Tyler–

recommended testing a descendant of another Tyler–Burke child. That step could have
taken weeks or months and would not have led directly to Bryan Kohberger, because he is
descended from a different sibling altogether.29

Instead, shortly after a verbal communication between David Mittelman of Othram and
Matthew Gamette of Idaho State Police Forensic Services, Idaho and federal law
enforcement asked the FBI Investigative Genetic Genealogy West Region Team to help
with the case.30 The FBI’s Los Angeles team began building family trees on 13 December
2022 and had named Bryan Kohberger as a suspect by 19 December 2022.31

In my opinion, the FBI identified Mr. Kohberger in just six days because they violated the
Department of Justice policy on FGG, as well as the Terms of Service for multiple
databases, and uploaded a modified DNA profile under a fictitious name to databases or
database portals they were forbidden to use.

I came to this conclusion based on several pieces of evidence.

     1. Two SNP profiles were provided in the discovery materials, one labeled “Othram
        Profile” and one labeled “FBI SNP Profile.” They are not the same, and the defense
        does not have access to the protocols and procedures used to generate either file.
        The Othram file contains 637,469 SNPs while the FBI file contains 1,543,086
        SNPs. Othram uploaded their file to FamilyTreeDNA and GEDmatch Pro on or
        before 8 December 2022. Because the file was already in the databases allowed
        by DOJ policy, there was no need for a second DNA data file.

     2. Although there was no need for a second DNA data file, the FBI appears to have
        modified Othram’s file using bioinformatics—more than doubling its size—
        presumably so this manipulated file could be uploaded to the same or other

          6-7 days old by the time the screenshot was taken on 14 December 2022.
          However, the forensic kit in the screenshot had been in the GEDmatch database for
          only one day.** It does not appear to be the same kit that Othram uploaded.

            their preliminary report rather than focusing on more distant matches and
            recommending a prolonged strategy to advance the case.

         list at 3,000, and I typically see 3,000–6,000 matches at FamilyTreeDNA for

Genetic Genealogy Analysis in This Case

As noted above, the two DNA matches that Othram reported (RK & HS) led to Clark Lewis
Tyler (1842–1910) and his wife Ellen Burke (1847–1927). They were the 2nd great
grandparents of RK and HS and the 3rd great grandparents of Bryan Kohberger. They
potentially have hundreds of living descendants who would match RK and HS at 70.7 cM
and 60 cM, respectively. (A third match at 36 cM is the first cousin of RK.)

A single DNA match, JS, helped to narrow the search to Mr. Kohberger’s great
grandparents. Although the Defendant’s Fifth Motion to Compel Discovery (15 April
2024, Item #15) requested the name of each database from which each match was
identified, that information was not provided to the defense. JS was most likely found in
the MyHeritage database. I base that inference on the facts that Othram did not report this
match from the permitted databases (FamilyTreeDNA and GEDmatch Pro) and that
MyHeritage has more than twice as many layperson DNA profiles as both FamilyTreeDNA
and GEDmatch combined. Both MyHeritage and the DOJ policy prohibit the use of this
database for forensic searches.

One other DNA match was used to focus the search on Mr. Kohberger’s grandparents. AV
was reported to share 107 cM with the forensic sample. I believe AV tested also at
MyHeritage for the reasons described above. I have two other concerns about this match.
First, AV is of Italian descent, and many Italians are from endogamous regions. Endogamy
can cause matches to share more DNA than expected based on the closest relationship.
Second, in my experience, the matching algorithm at MyHeritage often inflates matches,
reporting more shared DNA than other databases for the same two individuals. In other

37
   The MyHeritage Terms and Conditions in effect as of 9 Nov 2022 read: “using the DNA Services for law
enforcement purposes, forensic examinations, criminal investigations, "cold case" investigations, identification of
unknown deceased people, location of relatives of deceased people using cadaver DNA, and/or all similar purposes,
is strictly prohibited, unless a court order is obtained. It is our policy to resist law enforcement inquiries to protect
the privacy of our customers.” (https://web.archive.org/web/20230104022532/https://www.myheritage.com/terms-
and-conditions : accessed 4 Jan 2025)
38
   Bates 15841


Larkin: Idaho v. Kohberger report                                                                                     11
                                                         003240
words, it is possible that AV shares 107 cM with the forensic sample not because there is a
direct relationship but because they have multiple distant ancestors from the same region
in Italy, because of MyHeritage’s algorithm, or both.

One way to evaluate whether endogamous matches are related within the timeframe
proposed is to consider not just the total amount of shared DNA but also the number of
shared DNA segments and the size of the longest segment. Although this information was
requested in Defendant’s Fifth Motion to Compel Discovery (15 April 2024, Item #13), it
was not provided.

No matches to the forensic sample were related through Bryan Kohberger’s mother. In
other words, even if the matches to JS and AV were obtained legitimately, and even if the
match to AV was not affected by endogamy, the FGG search did not identify Mr.
Kohberger. Several other men in the extended Kohberger family fit those DNA matches.

To summarize, FGG is a multidisciplinary process that can involve multiple entities,
dozens of analysts, and many opportunities for error or miscommunication. A forensic
investigator typically samples the crime scene. The laboratory analyses (microarray or
WGS) and bioinformatics are outsourced to private, for-profit companies whose standard
operating procedures, protocols, software, and error rates are often proprietary. Each
DNA database has its own matching and ethnicity algorithms. DNA-based relationship
estimation is inherently imprecise. And genetic genealogists have different skill levels.
CeCe Moore, a leader in the field, has described FGG as “the Wild West” because of the
lack of accountability, independent oversight, and professional and ethical standards.39

For a robust defense, the accused should have complete access to all records and data that
should have been preserved from every phase of an FGG analysis. Mr. Kohberger’s
defense needs to know how the DNA data files were generated. The defense needs to
know which genealogy databases were used. The defense needs to know whether
endogamy is impacting the DNA interpretation. The defense needs to contact the DNA
matches to confirm their relationships and consent to FGG matching. And the defense
needs to know whether the Department of Justice interim policy on FGG was violated.



In conclusion, my review of the discovery thus far indicates that Othram’s genealogists
could not identify Mr. Kohberger. The FBI then took over the case, modified the original
SNP data file, and uploaded their version to forbidden databases in violation of the DOJ
policy and the Terms of Service of those databases. The FBI would not have identified Mr.
Kohberger so quickly had they followed protocol.

On January 3, 2023, I was retained by attorneys representing Bryan Kohberger to evaluate, consult and
provide a scene reconstruction of the event recorded as Moscow Police Department case #22-M09903.
Documentation was provided that included police reports, scene photographs, scene video, 3D
documentation, autopsy reports with photos, witness statements and forensic laboratory reports with notes.

This report outlines the findings associated with the evaluation of the submitted material. Representative
images of specific sample numbers or specific areas included in this report can be found in Appendix “A”.
See appendix “E” for a list of materials considered for this report.

        This assessment was conducted with the materials and information provided. Should
        additional relevant information or evidence become available, or if the direct examination
        of additional physical evidence related to this event is conducted, a supplemental report
        may need to be generated to incorporate the new information or evidence.

Background

On November 13, 2022, Dylan Mortensen called 911 and reported her roommate was passed out. Moscow
Police responded to 1122 King Road in Moscow, ID and identified four deceased people in the residence.
Each of the four deceased, Kaylee Goncalves, Madison Mogen, Ethan Chapin and Xana Kernodle, died
from multiple sharp force injuries.

Scene Visitation/Evidence Evaluation

During the course of this examination, I made three in person visits to the residence at 1122 King Road in
Moscow, Idaho. On January 3, 2023, I acquired photographs and multiple Faro 3D laser scans of the
interior. On January 27, 2023, I acquired additional photographs, additional 3D laser scans and collected
various locations of bloodstain patterns and other items (see Appendix “C”) to preserve for potential
additional examination due to anticipated destruction of the residence. On December 14, 2023, I took
additional photographs ahead of the scheduled destruction of the residence. During the December 14, 2023,
visit, most wall surfaces, flooring and other materials from the residence had been removed.

The 3D scans were registered using the computer program “Scene” to create a comprehensive 3D
environment of the interior of the residence. Two-dimensional top view diagrams were generated from the
3D scan data using the computer program “CadZone”. Mannequins to be used as placeholders for people
in the 3D environment were generated using the computer program “Poser”.

On June 29, 2023, select items of evidence recovered from the event were examined and photographed at
the office of Noedel Scientific to further document their condition.

Residence Characteristics and Scene Background

The residence was located at 1122 King Road in Moscow, Idaho. The residence was built into a hill and
had three levels with the front door on the north at the ground level, the second level accessible by a sliding
glass door located at the southwest corner of the house and the third level accessible via stairs in the interior
of the residence (see figure 1).

The interior of the house was arranged with the bottom floor (F1) positioned toward the north and connected
to the second floor (F2) by a set of stairs along the interior north wall. The top floor (F3) was positioned
toward the south and connected to floor two by a set of stairs toward the south. Floor two was the common
floor with the north half positioned over floor 1 and the south half positioned under floor 3 accessed via the
stairways at each end of the house (see figure 2).

Ethan Chapin and Xana Kernodle were discovered in the second-floor west bedroom. Kaylee Goncalves
and Madison Mogen were discovered in the third-floor east bedroom (see figure 3).

Two additional residents of the house were present during the murders. Dylan Mortensen occupied a
bedroom on the second floor east (across from the kitchen) and Bethany Funke occupied a bedroom on the
first floor east. Goncalves’ bedroom (3rd floor west) was found with the door open. Goncalves’ dog
(Murphy) was out of his kennel and on the bed in Goncalves’ bedroom (see figure 3a). The second floor
sliding glass door to the kitchen was found open upon first response.

The overall dimension of the residence was approximately 40 feet across (east/west) and 29 feet wide
(north/south). See figure 3b. Using the 3D data, the measured distance between the center of the second-
floor bedroom to the center of the third-floor bedroom was approximately 77 feet (including the set of stairs
connecting the second and third floors).

Dylan Mortensen was occupying the bedroom directly below where Goncalves and Mogen were found.
The stairs connecting the second and third floor are adjacent to her bedroom wall. She reported that she
saw a figure in the house as she looked out of her bedroom door around the time of this event (see figure
3c).

Bethany Funke occupied the bottom floor east bedroom. In her police interview, she did not recall anything
out of the ordinary except “she heard what she thought was a firework and saw a spark under her door”.
Mortensen and Funke were communicating via text and ultimately Mortensen reported going down to
Funke’s room after seeing a figure outside of her bedroom.

By noon the next day, Mortensen reported calling Emily Alandt and she along with Hunter Johnson (and
others) arrived to check the residence. Johnson discovered the body of Kernodle, armed himself with a
knife from the kitchen and then had Mortensen report the incident via a 911 call.
