        Sequence of Police Response and Analysis

The call to police regarding this event occurred just before noon on November 13, 2022. Initially, Dylan
Mortensen called a friend to come and check the status of the roommates. Hunter Johnson arrived (with
others) and went inside and discovered Kernodle and Chapin deceased in Kernodle’s bedroom. Hunter
Johnson went back into the residence when Moscow Police (Officers Nunes) arrived.

During the initial response, Moscow Police began to photograph and document the scene. Officer Nunes
was instructed to close the 3rd floor bedroom door to prevent the dog from entering that bedroom.
Ultimately, the dog was removed from the scene. During the initial police response, witness Johnson told
Officer Warner that he had retrieved a knife from the kitchen for protection while checking the victim’s
bedroom.

On November 13, 2022, (around 17:00 hours) Idaho State Police Detective Talbott and Prosecuting
Attorneys Bill Thompson and Ashley Jennings toured the residence. Detective Talbott acquired 3D scans
of the two bedrooms where deceased victims were located and Detective Talbott, Detective Powell and
Detective Schwecke marked evidence while Detective Roberts photographed the exhibits. This group
acquired numerous blood samples by swabbing from locations within the residence and those samples were
turned over to Detective Payne.

On November 14, 2022, Detective Talbott and the Idaho State Police D2 Investigation personnel returned
for further processing. Information provided included that rooms were searched, items removed to
secondary locations and then placed back into the rooms they were removed from.

On November 17 and 18, 2022, Idaho State Police Forensic Services (ISPFS laboratory) personnel were
called to the scene for processing and evidence collection. The notes from the ISPFS laboratory report
document that many items had been moved from their original locations, and that they documented the
scene as it appeared after the original removal and replacement of various items in the residence.

On January 3, 2023, this author toured the residence and acquired 3D scan data to be able to generate a “to-
scale” scene map not previously provided. Most areas of the residence were disheveled, and items had been
moved from their original locations, stacked on the victim’s beds and repositioned from their original
locations (see figures 4 and 4a).

On January 6, 2023, at the request of attorney Anne Taylor, Detective Talbott collected further evidence
including the beds, bedding, pillows and other involved bloodstained furniture or evidence from the
residence.

On October 31 and November 1, 2023, the FBI Evidence Response Team Unit reportedly completed
multiple 3D scans and photographs of the residence and surrounding area.

Bloodstain Pattern Analysis (See Appendix “A”)

For purposes of this report, stains visually consistent with blood or stains connected to areas that tested
positive for blood will all be considered as blood unless otherwise described. See Appendix A at the end of
this report for images and descriptions of each specific bloodstain. A glossary of bloodstain terms is
presented at the end of this report. A diagram of the residence mapping select DNA results is present in
Appendix “B”.

The initial bloodstain areas cataloged by Detective Talbott were identified in scene images with white
cardboard numbered placards. Many of these areas were sampled onto swabs. Detective Talbott identified
swab blood samples as scene placards #23 through #49. These swabs were then turned over to Detective
Payne who renumbered the swabs as items 17 through 43.

Then on November 17, 2022, Idaho State Police Forensic Services Laboratory (ISPFS laboratory) personnel
were asked to help process the scene and test the previously labeled areas with a presumptive blood test (o-
tolidine). The ISPFS laboratory was directed to the locations of the previously collected areas and identified
these locations with new yellow numbered stickers applied to the areas (matching the Talbott placard
numbers). The individual areas tested by the ISPFS laboratory had already been altered from the initial
swab collection.

The ISPFS laboratory personnel located additional stains and groups of patterns, each of which were
identified with yellow alphabet stickers.

    •   Samples that were ultimately tested in the forensic laboratory received new laboratory numbers and
        the notes associated with the new laboratory numbers reference the Detective Payne renumbering
        system. Assuming Detective Payne kept the same sequence of blood swab samples as Detective
        Talbott, one must add “6” from the Payne item number to get the Talbott on-scene “placard”
        number (i.e. Payne item 17 is Talbot scene placard 23). ISPFS laboratory notes, scene images and
        descriptions support the sequence used by Detective Talbott was maintained in the Payne
        renumbering.

Multiple stains and areas were tested by the ISPFS laboratory for the presence of blood using the
presumptive reagent “o-tolidine” with positive results. Many areas were further examined using DNA
techniques to identify the source of specific blood samples acquired from the scene. Appendix “B” at the
end of this report outlines the known results from DNA testing for specific stains sampled inside the
residence.

        General Reconstruction and Interpretations-3rd Floor Bedroom

Kaylee Goncalves was located on the north side of the 3rd floor bed where she was found next to Madison
Mogen. Three large saturation stains were on the pillow adjacent to Goncalves (to her north). Spatter on
the north wall adjacent to the bed (areas BC-BD) and blood pooling on the comforter in the vicinity of her
lap indicate that Goncalves was in a sitting up position at some point after receiving a bloodletting wound.
The autopsy report documented lacerations/blunt force injuries to the occipital scalp, an area which would
be exposed to injury while Goncalves was in a forward/bent position. Spatter extending laterally and above
the surface of the bed (areas BA, BB and BE) and onto the ceiling above that area (BM) suggest side and
overhead swings/motion of a bloody object. Goncalves’ final position was supine on the bed and with her
legs mostly extended under the quilt and her upper torso partially over the top of the right side of Madison
Mogen. Kaylee Goncalves did not move from the bed after receiving blood producing wounds.

Madison Mogen was located on the south side of the 3rd floor bedroom bed face up on the bed surface with
her lower torso under the covers. Mogen’s left leg was exposed off of the south side of the bed with her left
foot flat on the floor. A KA-BAR knife sheath was partially covered and tucked under the folded comforter
near her left hip. Spatter on the pillow behind her head and the walls and furnishings adjacent all support
that Mogen did not move her upper body much (if at all) after blood producing wounds were generated and
did not move from the bed itself after receiving blood producing wounds.

A cast-off pattern was observed on the west facing side of the closet (area BK). The presence of this pattern
represents where an object wet with blood was swung relatively horizontally from a location west of the
plane of the west side of the closet wall. This would position a person creating the cast-off at least 4 feet
west of the east wall (toward the foot of the bed area) to be in a location to create this cast-off pattern in
this location (see figure 5).

Two transfers of blood were documented on the edge of the door for the 3rd floor bedroom located between
4 and 5 feet up from the floor (areas “48” and “X”). This demonstrates that an object or objects wet with
blood was “mobile” in the scene to transfer blood from the victims to the door edge. Of note is that the
upper bloodstain (#48) matched the reference sample of Goncalves alone and the lower bloodstain (area
“X”) was a mixed profile from both Goncalves and Mogen. No dilution was represented in these stains.

    •   This area represents one or more direct contacts of a bloody source to the door edge (see figure 6).

        Laboratory Testing Knife Sheath
The knife sheath was tested at the Idaho State Police Forensic Services Laboratory (ISPFS laboratory) with
the following results:

    •   Area 1.1 was designated as a swab collection from the strap and buckle area at the upper end of the
        sheath. Ultimately, this sample was connected to Bryan Kohberger via DNA comparison.

    •   Area 1.2 was designated as a second swab that specifically rubbed the edges of the handle portion
        of the sheath. The recovered DNA from this process revealed a partial profile mixture of three
        individuals, at least one of which was male. The amount of DNA recovered was reported to be
        insufficient for comparison.

    •   Area 1.3 was designated as a third swab that specifically rubbed the edge of the external blade
        portion of the sheath. The recovered DNA from this process revealed a partial profile mixture of
        two individuals, at least one of which was male. The amount of DNA recovered was insufficient
        for comparison.

    •   Area 1.4 were swabs of the very small spatter bloodstains on the back of the sheath (the side
        exposed and facing up in the scene). These swabs were combined and found to have DNA from
        both Goncalves and Mogen.

    •   Area 1.5 was described as a swab of the inside surface of the blade portion of the sheath. The
        amount of DNA recovered was insufficient for comparison.

        Diluted Bloodstain Analysis Second Floor, Multiple Locations
                                               -




Note: For purposes of this report, diluted stains visually consistent with blood or stains connected to areas
that tested positive for blood that had a diluted appearance will all be considered as dilute bloodstains unless
otherwise described.

On the second floor of the residence, numerous areas of diluted bloodstains were documented (see figure
12). A diluted bloodstain is a type of blood deposit where the blood has been mixed with a second liquid
that gives the bloodstains a faint, light color appearance relative to the dark red/brown stain commonly seen
with undiluted blood.




 Figure 12: The 3D documentation of the second floor with some of the individual areas of
 diluted blood deposits marked with the scene label identifiers.

arranged as a "beer pong" table. The north end of the table had a collection of ten red plastic cups arranged
in a triangular formation; the south end of the table had three red plastic cups on the table and seven
additional cups were observed on the floor adjacent to the south table location. The specific upsetting of
the cups at the south side of the table represents where an action displaced the south side cups generally
toward the east, but did not significantly disturb the cups on the north side of the table.

        General Reconstruction and Analysis- 2nd floor Kernodle Bedroom

Ethan Chapin was discovered on the bed in the 2nd floor west bedroom. He was on his back diagonally
across the bed with his head toward the pillows at the southwest corner. His mid-section was covered with
a blue blanket and a pink comforter was co-mingled within the blanket covering him. The majority of the
bloodstains and blood pooling in this area support that he did not move far from this relative location while
bleeding. Chapin did not move off of the bed after receiving blood producing wounds.
Xana Kernodle was located on her back on the floor of the 2nd floor west bedroom. Of the four victims,
she was the only one who was not located in a bed or covered up. Bloodstains between the side of the bed
extending toward the north are generally low to the ground (such as transfers on the Coors box, the trash
can under the study table (Area “T”) and on the side of the nightstand (sample #32). The distribution and
locations of the bloodstains support that she was mobile between the north side of the bed and her final
location during the attack.


        Diluted Blood – Kernodle Bedroom
The presence of diluted bloodstains on the exterior door (Area Q) on the wall adjacent to the door (sample
29) and on the wall above the location of Chapin (scene MN-A) are consistent in appearance to the stains
on the pony (half) wall area (see figure 15). This supports that a source of diluted blood similar to that
which was present in the living room area, may also be connected to stains around the bedroom door area
and above Chapin’s area within the Kernodle bedroom.

    •   The deposit around the light switch (Sample #29) is consistent with spatter where the diluted blood
        landed adjacent to the light switch (rather than a contact onto or operating the switch itself). The
        diluted blood on the exterior door (Area “Q”) is at approximately the same height as the deposit
        around the light switch but exhibits a greater volume and more irregular distribution with passive
        flows down the door (see figure 16).

Diluted blood was on the south wall approximately 3 to 4 feet above the location of Ethan Chapin’s head
(see figure 17). This area was designated by this author as “Scene MN-A”. Blood in this specific area
supports that an object with a source of diluted blood deposited the spatter onto the wall above Chapin’s
location. This spatter was not specifically sampled or identified.

No additional areas of diluted spatter were observed in this room.

        Source of Dilution to Blood
Consideration by this author was made as to the source of dilution with inconclusive results. No evidence
of clean up was documented in any of the sinks anywhere in the residence and no “trail” of diluted drops
was documented in the scene processing connecting the kitchen or bathrooms to the diluted bloodstain
areas. The source of the dilution to blood or the reason blood became diluted remains unknown.

In the textbook “Principles of Bloodstain Pattern Analysis”, the authors wrote:
     “In some situations, the assailant or the victim may bathe. Tubs, showers and drains should be
     examined for such evidence.”
Collection of this type of evidence has been reported to be useful in the published scene examination
literature and the degree to which this was considered in relation to the apparent dilution in this event is
unknown.

    •   Three stains (samples 23, 26 and 27) on the pony (half) wall and stair area were tested by the ISPFS
        Laboratory and each sample was reported to be a DNA mixture of two people that matched
        Goncalves and Mogen. This evidence supports that a person who had blood from both Goncalves
        and Mogen from the 3rd floor became diluted and was then cast onto the pony (half) wall area of
        the 2nd floor.

    •   The stain from placard #39 was reported as a single source profile matching Goncalves. This
        indicates the diluted blood source was not uniform – that is, some deposits were a mix of both
        Goncalves and Mogen and at least one deposit (#39) was from Goncalves alone.

    •   The diluted stains on the door (Area Q) and light switch (Sample #29) were not identified and
        cannot be sourced to a specific individual. Mechanisms other than blood diluted from the mouth
        and nose of a victim should be considered.

    •   The diluted stain on the wall above Chapin’s location (Scene MN-A) was not sampled or tested.

Searches of Bryan Kohberger’s Vehicle and Residence

Records of the FBI search of Bryan Kohberger’s vehicle (Hyundai Elantra, WA plate # CFB8708)
conducted on December 30, 2022, resulted in the taking of swabs for potential DNA transfers from at least
55 locations, collection of items in the vehicle such as floor mats and seat belts, a series of vacuum filtration
samples for the collection of trace evidence and the use of a luminol formulation (a reagent that luminesces
when blood is detected in very dilute concentrations) and did not develop any connections through these
techniques to the four victims at the King street location.

    •   Figure 25 is a sketch of the areas tested during this car search. Included in the identifiers sketched
        in figure 25 were samples such as receipts, gloves, hiking boots, a shovel, goggles, all four floor
        mats, a door panel, seat covers/cushions, seat belts, head rests, part of the headliner, brake pedal
        cover, gas pedal and approximately 70 swabs of surfaces including seats, floors, trunk, exterior
        door handles, interior door handles driver’s seat adjustment lever, steering wheel, arm rests, parking
        brake, gear shift, radio controls, heater controls, gas and trunk release, and similar potential transfer
        areas.

    •   Hairs were recovered from the vacuum filtration systems and directly compared to the samples
        from the victims and the victims surviving dog – all with negative results. See FBI lab reports 2023-
        00090-12 Trace - Hairs/Fibers-3/2/2023.

    •   The comprehensive search of Bryan Kohberger’s vehicle did not locate any blood or specific
        evidence in connection with the events that took place at 1122 King Road.
On December 30, 2022, representatives from the Idaho State Police Forensic Services Laboratory examined
Bryan Kohberger’s apartment at 1630 NE Valley Rd #G201 in Pullman, WA. In total, the search resulted in
testing 51 positions in the apartment for indications of blood with only four of these indicating presumptive
positive for the presence of blood, none of which connected to the victims at the King Street residence and
all four of which were consistent with the known reference sample of Kohberger’s own DNA.
The amount of collective blood distributed within the scene supports that inadvertent, secondary transfers
of blood would be highly likely. Smudges, smears and transfers of blood seen on the third-floor door, stair
rail and walls, the second-floor rail and in the room of Kernodle are indicators that an assailant had received
blood onto themselves or onto objects they possessed.
Secondary transfers of blood are common when a particularly bloody scene is encountered. Because these
transfers are known to occur regularly, such secondary transfers of blood are purposefully sought during
crime scene processing and evaluation.
In the textbook “Principles of Bloodstain Pattern Analysis”, the authors wrote:
        “ Smudges, wipes, and transfer patterns of victim’s blood are frequently produced on and
        within an assailant’s vehicle while leaving the scene. Door handles, steering wheel,
        gearshift apparatus, console, and floor pedals should be examined carefully for these types
        of bloodstains.”



                                                Page 40 of 134

                                                     003287
                      Scene Reconstruction: State of Idaho v. Bryan Kohberger
                                        Noedel Scientific Report



The reason such a detailed examination and testing protocol is warranted is that the types of transfers occur
frequently enough to make them a routine part of a scene search. The FBI laboratory examined and tested
the vehicle, and the Idaho State Police Forensic Services Laboratory examined the Kohberger apartment in
Pullman, WA without finding any connection to the blood-letting that occurred at the King Road residence.

Rebuttal – T. Paulette Sutton Report

A forensic report issued August 29, 2024, by T. Paulette Sutton examined the bloodstains documented from
the examination of this event. The following specific areas are included here to provide further
interpretation or assessment considerations beyond what was presented in the Sutton report.

[1]       Sutton Report (page 10) – “It should be noted that there were no drip trails of blood noted on the
          bedroom floor. Drip trails are indicative of movement by a bleeding individual.”

Noedel Comment: Drip trails, when present, can represent movement of a bleeding person – or movement
of an object with wet blood of sufficient volume to continue to drip after blood acquisition (i.e. a bloody
weapon can create a drip trail from the weapon being carried away from a blood source).

[2]       Sutton Report (page 22) –

          (A) “Marker 42 in image DSC_4585 and DSC_4587 depicts a patterned transfer stain near the
          hinge side of the exterior surface of the 3rd level bedroom door.”

          (B) “A patterned transfer is created when a patterned object which was wet with liquid blood made
          contact with the surface. The appearance of this stain is consistent with diluted blood creating this
          patterned transfer. Diluted blood is created when blood is mixed with another liquid.”

          (C) “Subsequent testing at Marker 42 showed the DNA of Kaylee Goncalves.”

Noedel Comment:

      (A) This stain (as depicted in the Sutton report image 4587) is an altered bloodstain. The appearance
          depicted in this image represents what was left of the stain after the initial sampling conducted by
          Detective Talbott.

      (B) Original images of this stain show it to be small spatter (black and white numbered placard #42 of
          Talbott). The sample was then collected (likely with excessive water applied to the swab) altering
          the original appearance of the stain. Days later when the ISPFS laboratory processed the scene, a
          yellow sticker “42” was placed and the after-collection appearance photographed (see figure 26).

      (C) This stain was never DNA tested and therefore it cannot be attributed as originating from any
          specific individual. The misidentification of this sample may be associated with the renumbering
          system employed by Detective Payne.

Conclusions

Each victim had bloodstains surrounding their location supporting that after the fatal wounds were
delivered, none of the victims moved a significant distance (or not at all) from the area in which they were
located. No bloody “drip trails” were documented leaving the bedrooms.

Madison Mogen had received multiple sharp force wounds while lying on the south side of the bed in her
3rd floor bedroom. She did not move off of the bed after receiving blood producing wounds. Therefore, all
blood from her found outside the bedroom or in contact transfer locations where she could not touch must
have been deposited by a secondary source carrying her blood away from her position.

    •   A KA-BAR brand knife sheath was located face down and partially exposed adjacent to Mogen’s
        left hip. No specific knives or other sharp edge weapons have ever been recovered that are known
        to connect to any of the wounds documented in this event.

    •   The bloodstain at #41 on the top rail near the third floor is a location where blood sourced to Mogen
        was removed from the bedroom area and deposited by a source wet with her blood.

    •   Mogen was additionally represented in dilute bloodstains documented on the second-floor pony
        (half) wall area.

Kaylee Goncalves received blunt force injuries and sharp force wounds and was found adjacent to and
partially laying on Madison Mogen toward the north side of the bed in the Mogen 3rd floor bedroom. Her
body position changed during the attack (at some point bending forward while in the bed) but she did not
move from the bed surface after receiving bloodletting wounds. Therefore, all blood from her found outside
the bedroom or in contact transfer locations where she could not touch must have been deposited by a
secondary source carrying her blood away from her position.

    •   The bloodstains on the bedroom door at positions #48, area “X” on the 3rd floor and diluted stains
        on the beer pong table (#39), the pony (half) wall and adjacent stairway on the second floor are
        locations where blood sourced to Goncalves was removed from the 3rd floor bedroom area and
        deposited in various other locations.

Ethan Chapin received multiple sharp force wounds while lying on the bed in the southwest corner of
Kernodle’s 2nd floor bedroom. Although his body position changed during the attack, he did not move from
the bed after receiving bloodletting wounds.

    •   The bloodstain on the pony (half) wall at area “D” was sourced to Chapin.




                                              Page 46 of 134

                                                   003293
                      Scene Reconstruction: State of Idaho v. Bryan Kohberger
                                        Noedel Scientific Report



Conclusions continued

Xana Kernodle had received sharp force wounds and was found on the floor in her 2nd floor bedroom.
Bloodstains on surrounding surfaces indicate that she was mobile between the side of the bed and her final
position while low to the floor. Her location at the initiation of the attack is unknown. Her blood was not
identified beyond the interior threshold of her bedroom door.

ASB Definitions used in this report:

altered stain
A bloodstain with characteristics that indicate a physical change has occurred.

bloodstain
A deposit of blood on a surface.

bloodstain pattern
A grouping or distribution of bloodstains that indicates through regular or repetitive form, order, or
arrangement the manner in which the pattern was deposited.

cast-off pattern
A bloodstain pattern resulting from blood drops released from an object due to its motion.

cessation pattern
A bloodstain pattern resulting from blood drops released from an object due to its abrupt
deceleration.

directionality
The characteristic of a bloodstain that indicates the direction blood was moving at the time of
deposition.

drip pattern
A bloodstain pattern resulting from a liquid that dripped into another liquid, at least one of which
was blood.

drip stain
A bloodstain resulting from a falling drop that formed due to gravity.

drip trail
A bloodstain pattern resulting from the movement of a source of drip stains between two points.

flow
A bloodstain resulting from the movement of a volume of blood on a surface due to gravity or
movement of the target.

impact pattern
A bloodstain pattern resulting from an object striking liquid blood.

perimeter stain
An altered stain consisting of its edge characteristics, the central area having been partially or
entirely removed.

pool
A bloodstain resulting from an accumulation of liquid blood on a surface.


                                            Page 49 of 134

                                                 003296
                    Scene Reconstruction: State of Idaho v. Bryan Kohberger
                                     Noedel Scientific Report



saturation stain
A bloodstain resulting from the accumulation of liquid blood in an absorbent material.

spatter stain
A bloodstain resulting from an airborne blood drop created when external force is applied to liquid
blood.

swipe
A bloodstain resulting from the transfer of blood from a blood-bearing surface onto another
surface, with characteristics that indicate relative motion between the two surfaces.

transfer stain
A bloodstain resulting from contact between a blood-bearing surface and another surface.

void
An absence of blood in an otherwise continuous bloodstain or bloodstain pattern.

wipe
An altered stain resulting from an object moving through a preexisting wet bloodstain.

Madison Mogen Bedroom

This room was the location of both Madison Mogen and Kaylee Goncalves. Both were located on the bed
and had received multiple stab and laceration wounds. The surface of the bed was approximately 25 inches
up from the floor. The following observations were highlighted from the examination of the data from this
room.

        Sample #42
On the exterior side of the 3rd floor east bedroom door, area 42 was two small (approximately 1-2mm
diameter) individual drops. Below the two circular drops are a set of three small elliptical drops. These are
likely one or more deposits originating from inside the bedroom that were cast to this location including
possible cessation cast-off from a back swing of a bloody object.
        Area “X”
On the edge of the 3rd floor bedroom door are deposits called #48 and area “X”. Sample #48 is the higher
of two areas (about 56 inches up from floor) with area “X” about 50 inches up from the floor. Both are
swipes of a bloody object against the edge of the door. The swipes exhibit contact of an object wet with
blood moving across the door.
        Sample #48
On the edge of the 3rd floor bedroom door are deposits called #48 and area “X”. Sample #48 is the higher
of two areas (about 56 inches up from floor) with area “X” about 50 inches up from the floor. Both are
swipes of a bloody object against the edge of the door. The swipes exhibit contact of an object wet with
blood moving across the door.
        Area “BA”
On the west side of the north wall of the 3rd floor bedroom at the level of the light switch and above is an
area that contains overlapping small spatters visually consistent with blood. Many of the deposits have
directionality from east to west and may extend as far as the bedroom door.
        Area “BB”
On the west side of the north wall of the 3rd floor bedroom at the level of the light switch and below is an
area that contains overlapping small spatters visually consistent with blood. These deposits are consistent
with one or more overlapping cast-off patterns of blood representing where a bloody object was swung
across the level of the bed (a “horizontal” motion).
        Area “BC-BD” (sample #43)
This area is a complicated series of overlapping bloodstains on the north wall adjacent to the mid-section
of the bed. Spatter in this area is consistent with impacts to a bloody source essentially adjacent to this
location on the bed.
        Area “BE”

This area is located on the north wall near the east corner and toward the upper half of the wall above area
“BC-BD”. This area has a collection of impact and cast-off stains generated diagonally from the bed surface
toward the northeast corner.

        Area “BF”

This is a collection of bloodstains on the east wall above the bed. Many of these individual stains have
upward directionality and some were deposited onto the underside of the overhanging shelf.

Bloodstain Pattern Analysis – Second to Third Floor Stairs
Stairway between 2nd and 3rd Floors

Sample #41

On the top surface of the wooden banister adjacent to approximately the 3rd step down from the 3rd floor,
a contact transfer of blood and adjacent multi-directional swipe was documented. This represents a location
where an object wet with undiluted blood came in contact with the top of the banister surface.

Areas “N and O”

Located high on the east facing side of the central stair wall (below the top rail near Sample #41) are faint
transfers where an object with blood brushed or touched these two areas. Collectively, this area is consistent
with a person or object with blood on them touching the top and overhanging side of the banister in this
area possibly more than once and with some motion indicated (sample “O”).

where an object with wet blood brushed lightly against the face of the wall estimated to be approximately
2 feet above the floor.

Area “J”

This is a faint transfer above the banister on the west facing wall of the stairs (about 1.5 feet south of
Mortensen’s bedroom door). This represents where a bloody object lightly touched the wall in this location.

Collectively, these transfers support that someone with wet blood (or an object carrying wet blood) touched
or brushed against these areas.

Bloodstain Pattern Analysis – Second Floor Central
2nd Floor Living room and Hall Areas

The stairway connecting the first and second floor was centrally located along the north wall. The upper
half of the stairs was separated from the living room by a “pony (half) wall”. The pony (half) wall was
approximately 33 ½ inches tall and had a wooden rail along the top.

Areas “A, B, C”

These three stains were located on or near the upper half of the banister along the north wall connecting
floor 1 to floor 2. Stain “A” may be a single drop of spatter, while stains “B” and “C” are consistent with
contact transfers.

Area “D”

This deposit did not appear diluted and was located on the north edge of the top of the rail to the pony (half)
wall toward the east. This sample matched the DNA of Chapin and represents where someone with his
blood contacted the top of the rail area.

Area “E”

On top of pony (half) wall were dilute elliptical stains (at least three) originating from the south likely from
a cast of dilute blood toward the north.

Samples #23, #24, #25 and #26

These stains all have similar appearance and are representative of a source of diluted blood arriving from
southeast of the pony (half) wall and being cast-off eclipsing the south side of the pony (half) wall and over
the top to hit the north wall of the stairway.

    •   Stain 23 was located on the north wall of the stairwell and was a single drop consistent with a cast-
        off with enough volume to passively flow approximately 2 inches down the wall. The orientation
        of the drop indicates that it was moving from east to west and downward when it hit the wall. There
        are two smaller deposits below the large drop at stain 23 with a similar cast-off appearance.

    •   Stain 24 was located on the north wall of the stairwell and was a single diluted drop (approximately
        4mm and ovoid). The stain is likely a single drop of diluted cast-off originating from south of the
        stairway.

    •   Stain 25 was located on the south side of the pony (half) wall approximately 27 inches up from the
        floor. This was a group of three diluted drops (approximately 4mm) with enough volume to
        passively flow approximately 4 inches down the wall.

    •   Stain 26 was located on the south side of the pony (half) wall and was comprised of at least nine
        diluted drops (each approximately 4mm) some of which had passively flowed down the wall.




                                                Page 80 of 134

                                                    003327
                       Scene Reconstruction: State of Idaho v. Bryan Kohberger
                                         Noedel Scientific Report



Sample #27

On the east facing wall above the stairs, there was a darker (but still diluted) stain and two very dilute drops
with enough volume to passively flow down the wall.

Sample #28

This was a faint swipe across the north hall wall between the pony (half) wall and the door to Kernodle’s
room. This swipe was located approximately 48-55 inches up from the floor.

Areas “V-W”

These were two dilute deposits with associated passive flows down the wall. These deposits are consistent
with a cast-off arriving from east to west before passively flowing down the wall.

Areas “G-H-I” – Dilute bloodstains low on the baseboards in the hall adjacent to the pony (half) wall appear
diluted with an irregular shape.

Stain “F”

This single stain was a narrow drop of blood on the west facing side edge of the beer pong table in the living
room. This single stain has some dilute appearance and represents where a single drop was deposited from
adjacent to the table.

Sample #59

On the east facing wall of the living room low across from the beer pong table (approximately eight inches
up from the floor) were multiple dilute deposits, some with enough volume to passively flow down the
wall.

Sample #39

Sample #39 was located on the surface of the “beer pong” table is an irregular large single diluted deposit
(approximately 2 cm diameter) with a tail extending toward the north. This deposit is consistent with a
diluted drop of blood being cast generally from south toward north and landing on the table surface.

    •   A collection of diluted spatter stains was observed in photographs of the surface of a potato chip
        bag located on the couch adjacent to the (east of) the beer pong table. The appearance and color of
        this spatter is consistent with other diluted spatter documented in this area.

Footwear impression Developed with Amido Black

An apparent footwear impression developed with Amido Black was located on the floor outside of the
bedroom of Dylan Mortensen (second floor, bottom of stairs).

Bloodstain Pattern Analysis – Second Floor West
Xana Kernodle Bedroom

Area “AA” (Sample #34)

On the west wall of the room adjacent to the head of where Kernodle was located, was a pattern consistent
with one or more overlapping of cast-off patterns(including some deposits on the adjacent standing mirror).

    •   This area was located adjacent to (approximately 1.5 feet west of) the head of Kernodle and was
        likely generated when she was low to the ground in this area while being struck.

Sample #35

This location was consistent with a swipe and pattern transfer onto the southwest leg of the desk that was
centrally located against the north wall. These deposits were adjacent to the location of Kernodle and
represent where an object wet with blood brushed against the desk leg.

Area “AB”

On the central west wall centered approximately 25 inches up from the floor was a collection of spatters.

Area “AC”

On the west wall in the area between the floor and approximately 24 inches up the wall and between the
north edge of the bed and a nightstand, are a variety of different deposits of blood. In the area around 24 to
36 inches up is a collection of spatter. Within this area, are four, swipes through parts of the deposits on the
wall.

Sample #31

Below the secondary disturbance and approximately 12 inches up from the floor between the bed and a
nightstand is a large bloodstain with radiating spines indicative on an impact of a bloody source against the
wall.

    •   This represents where a source of wet blood hit against the wall, transferring blood at the contact
        point.

    •   At least two stab slits into the side of the bed were documented adjacent to this area, but no
        visible blood wipes were observed at the perimeter of the stabs to the bed.

Sample #32

This area was comprised of a complicated overlapping series of spatter, swipes and transfers on the side
and legs of a nightstand located along the west wall north of the bed. The orientation and multiple
directions observed in this collection of deposits indicates dynamic movement in this area from a source
(or sources) wet with blood.



                                                Page 98 of 134

                                                    003345
                      Scene Reconstruction: State of Idaho v. Bryan Kohberger
                                         Noedel Scientific Report



Sample #33

This area was comprised of a complicated and overlapping collection of stains on the floor east of the
nightstand (see stain 32). Included in this area is a circular stain (approximately 2 inches in diameter) that
may be from the bottom of a bottle (or similar cylindrical object).

    •   Documentation of this area by the ISPFS laboratory was sent to the Ada County Sheriff’s Office
        Forensic Lab to evaluate for potential footwear impressions. The Ada County lab report located
        impressions within this area that are “likely footwear impressions” (see Latah County Prosecuting
        Attorney report supplement 240).

Area “AD”

On the west wall above the bed are a group of spatter comprised of larger size drops, at least two of which
have enough volume to passively flow down the wall. There are two or three swipes of apparent blood
across the wall, some of which appear dilute representing a source wet with blood brushing across the west
wall above the bed.
Areas “AE”; “AF” and “AG” (Sample #30)
Primarily on the south wall and passively flowing down the wall to the floor are a collection of complicated
impact spatters, projections and swipes of blood. The saturation stains on the bed surface and large pooling
on the floor identified this was the location where Chapin had been located after receiving blood producing
wounds. Blood accumulated on the floor in this area seeped through the foundation and continued to
passively flow to the outside bulkhead of the house. The totality of the combination of bloodstains in this
area support that Chapin did not move much from the south side of the bed after receiving blood producing
wounds.
Area “Scene MN-A”
On the south wall above area “AE” is a collection of diluted bloodstains visually similar in color and
appearance to the dilute stains documented elsewhere on the middle floor.
Area “Q”
On the exterior side of the bedroom door is a linear collection of dilute blood deposits located approximately
48 inches up from the floor. This pattern represents a location where a source, wet with diluted blood,
created a cast-off and impact type pattern onto the door. A minor swipe across this area is consistent with
motion through the diluted blood source. A very long (approximately 3 feet) linear diluted passive flow
originates above the exterior knob and has sufficient volume to run nearly to the bottom of the door.
Sample #36
On the exterior side of the door are at least five large volume drops where blood with low energy is
“falling” downward from above and being intercepted by the door at the area below the exterior
doorknob.




                                               Page 99 of 134

                                                    003346
                       Scene Reconstruction: State of Idaho v. Bryan Kohberger
                                        Noedel Scientific Report



Sample #29
On the east wall adjacent to the bedroom door is a collection of at least twenty diluted droplets of spatter
moving from south toward north onto the east facing light switch on the wall inside Kernodle’s bedroom.
These deposits are visually consistent with the color and visual appearance as the deposits at position
“Q”.

Sample #37

On the floor west of the edge of the doorway is a single blood drop with altered stains adjacent.
Additional individual drops that had become “skeletonized” and then wiped through from secondary
movement were also documented in this area.

Area “R”

On the floor at the entryway to the bedroom was a collection of circular undiluted blood drops.

Area “S”

On the short east facing wall below sample #29 (near the floor) was a single blood drop that originated
from above.

Area “T”

This deposit was a swipe of blood presented as two parallel equal size swipes on the side of the
cylindrical trash can found under the desk in this room. This is indicative of an object wet with blood
swiping against the trash can.

Area “U”

On a low chair toward the northwest corner of the room (near sample #34) was a collection of transfer
stains on the white long hair rug adjacent to the area of Kernodle’s body.

Other Blood Deposits

    •   A Coors Light box with transfers of blood was documented on the floor adjacent to the body of
        Kernodle.

                                          KA-BAR Knife Review

RE: Ka-Bar Knife Documentation
State of ID v. Bryan Kohberger                                                                     1/21/2025

Introduction

During the course of the reconstruction of this event, many questions were raised about the potential
weapons used in this event. A KA-BAR, USMC brand leather sheath discovered adjacent to the
body of Madison Mogen initiated many questions about the dimensions and potential performance
of the type of knife marketed to go with that sheath.

To that end, a replica KA-BAR USMC brand knife (KA-BAR item 1217) was purchased to assess
and characterize the class characteristics of such a knife. Those evaluations are discussed in this
review.

Examinations

The design of KA-BAR knife represented by the recovered sheath has a blade length of approximately 7
inches, has a blade width of approximately 1 ¼ inches (that tapers to a point) and a blade thickness of
approximately 0.175 inches (see figure 1).




   Figure 1: A replica KA-BAR knife used for this assessment.


To evaluate the type of class characteristics a knife with the replica KA-BAR dimensions can achieve when
used to stab, test stabs were made into ballistic gelatine (Clear Ballistics) and the results documented. This
design of knife has a point at the end that tapers to a width of approximately 1.25 inches at its widest part
on the body of the blade (see figure 2)

    •   Testing conducted by stabbing into the gelatine showed that when a knife with these proportions
        was stabbed into a surface to a shallow depth, the width of the entry cut was narrow because the
        blade is narrower where it comes to a point. When the knife is stabbed deeply into the gelatine, the
        full width of the knife (approximately 1 ¼ inches) was represented on the width of the entry cut.
        The width of the entry cut may be wider than the width of the knife at any given stab depth (due to

                                                 Page 1 of 3


                                                   003382
                                                    mnoedel@att.net       (253) 227-5880
                                                                        www.noedelscientific.com

                                          KA-BAR Knife Review

RE: Ka-Bar Knife Documentation

       rocking the knife forward or back during stab or withdrawal). In addition, lacerations (lateral cuts)
       may not retain the dimensions of the stabbing instrument.

   •   Note-Ballistic gelatine is a uniform substance that is not designed to replicate the elasticity of living
       tissue.




 Figure 2: A replica KA-BAR knife measured showing a blade width of approximately 1.25
 inches at a distance of approximately 2 inches from the tip.



In this event there was a serrated type steak knife on the living room table reported to have been
acquired by a witness after the event. By way of comparison, a typical steak knife was stabbed
adjacent to the replica KA-BAR knife into ballistic gel and the resultant size of stab slit produced
is shown in figure 3.

                                 RACHEL L. ORR, PSYD. ABPP-CN

       Rachel L. Orr, Psyd. ABPP-CN, may testify for the defense as an expert regarding her

neuropsychological evaluation of Bryan Kohberger. Dr. Orr’s opinion/testimony will be

based on her experience, education, and trainings as detailed in her curriculum vitae which is

included with this response as Exhibit D-7C.

        This response serves to supplement the information in the Report attached as

Exhibit D7-B. The Dr. Orr’s anticipated testimony will be her opinions and methodology

consistent with all specific findings that are detailed in her report.

        Dr. Orr’s testimony is not intended to be a mental element defense pursuant to Idaho

Code 18-207; but rather this testimony about state of mind as well as factual defense testimony

to anticipated testimony elicited by the State.

        Dr. Orr may testify about findings, testing, impressions, and/or conclusions drawn

from the work of other experts who previously conducted evaluations/examinations or

provides conclusions relating to the field of neuropsychology as well as regarding testimony

offered by the State relating to psychology.


        Dr. Orr’s disclosure may be supplemented based on new information and disclosures

made by the State.

       This is a Phase One expert report and may be supplemented for Phase Two, in accordance

with the expert report deadline for the penalty phase.

                                 REASON FOR REFERRAL:

Bryan Kohberger is a 30-year-old male who is charged with four counts of murder in the first
degree and one count of burglary. He is referred for neuropsychological evaluation by his
defense team to characterize his functioning, assist with differential diagnosis, and provide
expert opinion to the court about the findings. Bryan was informed of the limits to confidentiality
and the nature and purpose of the evaluation. He consented to the evaluation.

  Item Q13.1        questioned sample from body of person A (Madison Mogen)

METHODS:

    •   The DNA PowerPlex® Fusion data profiles referenced in this report were previously developed by the Idaho State Police
        Forensic Services laboratory and addressed in case documentation issued by the Law Office of Bicka Barlow.
    •   The TrueAllele® Casework system processed each evidence item in independent replicate computer runs to infer possible
        DNA contributor genotypes from the samples.
    •   The National Institute of Standards and Technology generated the population allele frequencies.
    •   The DNA match statistics herein were calculated using VUIer™ version 3.3.8343.1R20b (26-Aug-2022) at a theta value (co-
        ancestry coefficient) of 1%.
    •   All evidence genotypes were compared with all reference genotypes to compute likelihood ratio (LR) DNA match statistics.
    •   The match comparisons described herein were requested for reporting by Anne Taylor Law, PLLC.

                                                            003475
Cybergenetics: BK
Lab: M2022-4843; Agency: 22-M09903
November 27, 2024

RESULTS:

TrueAllele assumed that the evidence sample data (Item Q13.1) contained three or four contributors, and objectively inferred evidence
genotypes solely from these data. Some evidence genotypes were inferred assuming known reference genotypes. Degraded DNA was
considered. Following genotype inference, the computer then compared separated genotypes from this evidence item with provided
reference genotypes (Items 11, 14, and 108), relative to ethnic populations, to compute LR DNA match statistics. Based on these
results:

A match between the body sample (Item Q13.1) and Madison Mogen (Item 11) is:
        614 nonillion times more probable than a coincidental match to an unrelated African-American person,
        460 octillion times more probable than a coincidental match to an unrelated Caucasian person, and
        57 octillion times more probable than a coincidental match to an unrelated Hispanic person.

         For a match strength of 57 octillion, only 1 in 424 nonillion people would match as strongly.

A match between the body sample (Item Q13.1) and Kaylee Goncalves (Item 14) is:
        124 billion times more probable than a coincidental match to an unrelated African-American person,
        11.1 billion times more probable than a coincidental match to an unrelated Caucasian person, and
        12.6 billion times more probable than a coincidental match to an unrelated Hispanic person.

         For a match strength of 11.1 billion, only 1 in 208 billion people would match as strongly.

A match between the body sample (Item Q13.1) and Bryan Kohberger (Item 108) is:
        2.18 billion times less probable than a coincidental match to an unrelated African-American person,
        2.8 billion times less probable than a coincidental match to an unrelated Caucasian person, and
        1.77 billion times less probable than a coincidental match to an unrelated Hispanic person.

         For an exclusionary statistic of one over 1.77 billion, only 1 in 104 billion people would be excluded as strongly.

TrueAllele® Casework Method


Computer interpretation of DNA evidence

A definite genotype can be determined when a person’s DNA produces unambiguous data. However, when the data signals are less
definitive, or when there are multiple contributors to the evidence, uncertainty arises. This uncertainty is expressed in the resulting
genotype, which may describe different genetic identity possibilities. Such genotype uncertainty may translate into reduced
identification information when a comparison is made with a suspect.

The DNA identification task can thus be understood as a two-step process:
  1. objectively inferring genotypes from evidence data, accounting for allele pair uncertainty using probability, and
  2. subsequently matching genotypes, comparing evidence with a suspect relative to a population, to express the strength of
     association using probability.
The match strength is reported as a single number, the likelihood ratio (LR), which quantifies the change in identification information
produced by having examined the DNA evidence.

The TrueAllele Casework system is a computer implementation of this two-step DNA identification inference approach. The
computer objectively infers genotypes from DNA data through statistical modeling, without reference to a known comparison
genotype. To preserve the identification information present in the data, the system represents genotype uncertainty using probability.
These probabilistic genotypes are stored on a relational database. Subsequent comparison with suspects provides evidentiary
identification information.

Over forty TrueAllele validation studies have been conducted to establish the reliability of the method [1]. Eight of these studies have
been published in peer-reviewed scientific journals, on both synthetic [2, 3, 4, 5, 6] and casework [7, 8, 9] data. There are related
papers on data analysis validation [10] and error reporting [11]. TrueAllele has been empirically tested and complies with six national
standards for validating probabilistic genotyping systems and other performance criteria, e.g., [12, 13].

Data
Quantitative peak data from STR experiments on biological evidence that were entered
as input for TrueAllele® computation.


Table

The data table shows the peak information for each evidence item. Each row gives
statistics for one peak. The columns describe the peak as:

The DNA template that includes the peak.

The track indicates the amplification(s) included in the template.

The locus that includes the peak.

The peak’s designation (i.e., number of repeats).

The base pair length of the peak.

The peak’s height in RFU values.

The area under the peak.

TrueAllele®	  Methods:	  Statistical	  Model	  


System	  3,	  Version	  25	  
September	  2008	  model	  


Mark	  Perlin,	  PhD,	  MD,	  PhD	  
Cybergenetics,	  Pittsburgh,	  PA	  
8	  March	  2016	  




Overview	  


This	  document	  provides	  scientific	  background	  and	  mathematical	  formulas	  for	  statistical	  
modeling	  in	  the	  TrueAllele	  system.	  	  The	  document	  complements	  previously	  published	  
descriptions	  of	  the	  hierarchical	  Bayesian	  model	  for	  genotype	  separation.	  	  	  


Data	  


Short	  tandem	  repeat	  (STR)	  data	  originate	  as	  charge-­‐coupled	  device	  (CCD)	  camera	  counts	  
that	  are	  collected	  on	  a	  genetic	  analyzer	  from	  fluorescently	  end-­‐labeled	  DNA	  fragments	  as	  
they	  are	  separated	  by	  size	  via	  gel	  electrophoresis.	  	  These	  multi-­‐spectral	  CCD	  signals	  are	  
isolated	  by	  their	  fluorescent	  dyes	  using	  a	  color	  separation	  matrix	  to	  form	  dye-­‐specific	  
signals	  via	  matrix	  inversion.	  	  	  
             Signal	  analysis	  identifies	  a	  DNA	  data	  peak	  corresponding	  to	  a	  particular	  DNA	  
fragment.	  	  Using	  allelic	  and	  internal	  size	  ladders,	  the	  analysis	  determines	  a	  DNA	  peak’s	  size	  
(bp)	  and	  allele	  length	  (repeats),	  as	  well	  as	  the	  DNA	  quantity	  measured	  in	  relative	  
fluorescent	  units	  (rfu).	  	  A	  data	  vector	  records	  the	  DNA	  quantity	  (including	  zero)	  for	  every	  
fragment	  size.	  	  	  




                                                                     1	  

                                                                  003635
            We	  model	  the	  quantitative	  data	  at	  STR	  locus	   l 	  (of	   L 	  loci)	  using	  several	  variables.	  	  
Data	  vector d l forms	  a	  pattern	  that	  maps	  DNA	  product	  lengths	  into	  their	  observed	  
quantitative	  peak	  heights.	  	  	  
            We	  linearly	  model	  the	  data	  vector	   d l 	  using	  a	  truncated	  ( ≥ 0 )	  multivariate	  normal	  
distribution	   N + 	  of	  the	  mean	  vector	   µl 	  and	  covariance	  matrix	   Σ l as	  

                                                                   d l ∼ N + ( µ l , Σl )

            We	  write	  the	  peak	  data	  covariance	  matrix	   Σ l 	  as	  

                                                                   Σl = σ 2 ⋅Vl + τ 2

where	   σ 2 	  is	  amplification	  dispersion,	   τ 2 	  is	  detection	  variation,	  and	   Vl 	  is	  a	  diagonal	  matrix	  

diag ( d l ) 	  of	  peak	  heights.


Data	  Usage	  


TrueAllele	  determines	  statistical	  parameters	  directly	  from	  the	  data,	  mining	  DNA	  evidence	  
for	  statistical	  information.	  	  The	  fully	  Bayesian	  system	  does	  not	  require	  calibration	  (i.e.,	  
setting	  parameters	  from	  historical	  laboratory	  data	  unrelated	  to	  evidence	  data).	  	  	  
            TrueAllele	  inputs	  and	  uses	  all	  the	  data.	  	  There	  are	  no	  thresholds,	  since	  uncertainty	  is	  
determined	  statistically	  from	  the	  data.	  	  There	  is	  an	  optional	  rfu	  cutoff,	  usually	  set	  at	  ten	  rfu	  
(within	  the	  background	  noise),	  well	  below	  allelic	  peak	  events.	  	  Should	  alleles	  be	  observed	  
below	  this	  level,	  the	  cutoff	  can	  be	  lowered	  or	  turned	  off.	  	  	  
            Allele	  dropout	  occurs	  when	  alleles	  that	  are	  present	  in	  the	  genotypes	  do	  not	  appear	  
in	  the	  data	  signal.	  	  Bayesian	  modeling	  accounts	  for	  all	  genotype	  possibilities,	  whether	  or	  
not	  component	  alleles	  manifest	  themselves	  in	  the	  genotyping	  data.	  	  TrueAllele	  assesses	  
allele	  dropout	  through	  a	  likelihood	  function,	  assigning	  lower	  probabilities	  to	  genotype	  
proposals	  that	  have	  less	  support	  in	  the	  data.	  	  TrueAllele	  addresses	  allele	  drop-­‐in	  events	  in	  a	  
similar	  way.	  	  There	  are	  no	  explicit	  drop	  parameters	  –	  Bayes	  theorem	  with	  an	  informative	  
likelihood	  function	  addresses	  data	  drop	  phenomena.	  	  	  
            Using	  all	  the	  data	  is	  thorough	  and	  preserves	  identification	  information.	  	  Eliminating	  
human	  data	  decisions	  (choosing	  loci,	  peaks,	  artifacts)	  removes	  human	  bias	  from	  the	  


                                                                               2	  

                                                                           003636
interpretation	  process.	  	  Users	  cannot	  “control	  their	  data.”	  	  The	  user	  supplies	  the	  data,	  
makes	  few	  assumptions	  (number	  of	  contributors,	  sampling	  time,	  degradation	  option),	  and	  
the	  rest	  is	  done	  automatically	  by	  the	  computer	  system.	  	  	  
           TrueAllele	  can	  answer	  questions	  about	  different	  data	  combinations.	  	  Data	  from	  
multiple	  items	  or	  amplifications	  can	  be	  used	  in	  a	  joint	  genotype	  analysis.	  	  Known	  genotypes	  
(e.g.,	  a	  victim	  present	  in	  a	  mixture,	  ascertained	  by	  case	  context	  or	  match	  statistics)	  can	  help	  
reduce	  problem	  complexity.	  	  	  
           A	  comparison	  genotype	  (e.g.,	  a	  suspect)	  cannot	  be	  part	  of	  interpreting	  evidence.	  	  
The	  computer	  does	  not	  know	  the	  “answer”	  when	  it	  separates	  genotype	  from	  evidence.	  	  A	  
match	  comparison	  is	  only	  made	  afterwards.	  	  Guaranteeing	  that	  genotype	  inference	  is	  
entirely	  separate	  from	  match	  statistic	  calculation	  helps	  ensure	  process	  objectivity.	  	  	  


Mass	  


DNA	  is	  packaged	  in	  the	  cell	  nucleus.	  	  This	  cell	  packaging	  is	  opened	  when	  DNA	  is	  extracted	  
from	  a	  biological	  sample	  and	  made	  available	  for	  laboratory	  analysis.	  	  The	  mass,	  or	  number	  
of	  intact	  DNA	  molecules	  examined	  in	  a	  test	  tube,	  is	  modeled	  as	  a	  normal	  random	  variable.	  	  	  
           The	  total	  DNA	  quantity	  at	  locus	   l 	  is	  given	  by	  mass	  parameter	   ml .	  	  	  The	  locus	  mass	  
ml 	  prior	  is	  a	  (nonnegative)	  truncated	  normal	  distribution	  on	  feasible	  total	  peak	  rfu	  values.	  	  

                                                           ml ∼ N + ( 5000, 5000 2 )


Genotype	  


Individuals	  inherit	  DNA	  from	  two	  parents.	  	  Therefore,	  at	  a	  given	  genetic	  locus	  on	  an	  
autosomal	  chromosome,	  a	  cell	  has	  two	  alleles	  (STR	  length	  variants),	  one	  from	  each	  parent.	  	  
This	  pair	  of	  alleles	  is	  called	  a	  genotype.	  	  A	  genotype	  is	  represented	  as	  a	  vector	  of	  all	  possible	  
allele	  sizes,	  with	  each	  vector	  entry	  containing	  a	  number	  of	  alleles	  at	  that	  particular	  size.	  	  	  
           With	   K 	  contributors	  to	  the	  data,	  we	  represent	  the	   k th 	  contributor	  genotype	  
parameter	  at	  locus	   l 	  as	  a	  vector	   g k,l ,	  where	  the	  DNA	  length	  entries	  contain	  allele	  counts	  



                                                                            3	  

                                                                        003637
that	  sum	  to	  1.	  	  A	  heterozygote	  genotype	  vector	   g k,l 	  contains	  two	  1/2	  entries,	  while	  a	  

homozygote	  has	  a	  single	  1	  entry;	  all	  other	  vector	  entries	  are	  0.	  	  	  
            The	  genotype	  prior	  probability	   Pr {g k,l = x} 	  at	  allele	  pair	   x = [i j ] 	  is	  a	  product	  of

population	  allele	  frequencies	   { fi } .

                                                                     ⎧ f 2, i = j
                                                                     ⎪ i
                                                             g k,l ∼ ⎨
                                                                     ⎪⎩ 2 fi f j , i ≠ j

            TrueAllele’s	  likelihood	  function	  assesses	  a	  genotype	  candidate	  value	  to	  determine	  
how	  well	  it	  explains	  the	  observed	  data.	  	  The	  likelihood	  is	  larger	  when	  the	  quantitative	  data	  
is	  better	  accounted	  for	  by	  a	  predicted	  peak	  height	  pattern	  based	  on	  the	  allele	  pair	  value.	  	  
For	  the	  ith	  data	  observation	   dl,i 	  at	  locus	  l,	  the	  likelihood	  function	  for	  a	  genotype	   g k,l 	  is	  the	  

probability	   Pr {dl,i | g k,l = x,...} 	  of	  the	  data	  conditioned	  on	  genotype	  value	  x,	  where	  "..."

denotes	  the	  other	  model	  variable	  values,	  given	  by	  the	  data	  distribution	   d l ∼ N + (µl , Σl ) .

            Combining	  the	  prior	  genotype	  probability	  together	  with	  I	  independent	  genetic	  data	  
observations,	  we	  can	  compute	  the	  posterior	  genotype	  probability	  using	  Bayes	  theorem	  as	  
the	  product	  of	  prior	  probability	  and	  joint	  likelihood	  functions.	  	  The	  probability	  mass	  
function	  (pmf)	   q ( x ) 	  of	  genotype	   g k,l 	  is	  the	  joint	  probability	  distribution

                         Pr {g k,l = x | dl,1 ,dl,2 ,...,dl,i ,...} ∝ Pr {g k,l = x} ⋅ ∏ Pr {dl,i | g k,l = x,...}

                                                                                                   i=1


over	  all	  the	  relevant	  random	  variables.	  


Mixture	  Weight	  


A	  mixture	  contains	  DNA	  from	  two	  or	  more	  people.	  	  The	  relative	  amount	  of	  DNA	  from	  a	  
person	  contained	  in	  the	  mixture	  is	  a	  mixture	  weight	  value	  between	  zero	  and	  one.	  	  The	  sum	  
of	  the	  mixture	  weights	  over	  all	  the	  people	  contributing	  the	  mixture	  is	  one.	  	  	  
            The	  mixture	  weight	  parameter	  at	  locus	   l 	  is	  a	  vector	   w l 	  whose	   K 	  contributor	  
                                                     K
components	  sum	  to	  1,	  so	  that	   ∑ wk,l = 1 .	  	  A	  hierarchical	  model	  of	  mixture	  weight	  at	  every	  
                                                     k=1

as	  a	  hierarchical	  prior	  from	  a	  common	  DNA	  template	  mixture	  weight	   w 	  using	  a	  truncated	  
(simplex)	  multivariate	  normal	  distribution	  as	  
                                                            w l ∼ N 0,1 K−1 ( w, ψ 2 ⋅ I )

Genotype	  Combination	  


Genotypes	  are	  combined	  in	  a	  mixture	  by	  adding	  together	  contributor	  vectors,	  with	  each

Amplification	  Variance	  


The	  polymerase	  chain	  reaction	  (PCR)	  is	  an	  imperfect	  copying	  mechanism.	  	  A	  PCR	  cycle	  does	  
not	  automatically	  double	  the	  number	  of	  copies	  of	  a	  particular	  DNA	  fragment.	  	  Rather,	  the	  
number	  of	  fragment	  copies	  randomly	  increases	  each	  round	  by	  a	  factor	  between	  one	  and	  
two.	  	  This	  random	  branching	  process	  follows	  the	  mathematics	  of	  a	  Poisson	  counting	  
process,	  which	  can	  be	  modeled	  as	  a	  positive-­‐valued	  distribution	  having	  a	  variance	  that	  
scales	  with	  fragment	  quantity! y 	  as	  !σ 2 ⋅ y .

                                                                         003639

distribution.	  	  	  
                                                                  σ −2 ∼ Gam (10, 20 ) 	  
	  
Background	  Variance	  
	  
Instrument	  noise	  arises	  from	  a	  genetic	  analyzer’s	  laser	  signal,	  optical	  path,	  CCD	  camera,	  
and	  other	  sources.	  	  This	  background	  noise	  is	  independent	  of	  the	  PCR	  process,	  and	  can	  be	  
modeled	  as	  a	  normal	  distribution	  having	  a	  fixed	  variance	  parameter.

distribution.

PCR	  Stutter	  
	  
The	  DNA	  polymerase	  enzyme	  can	  drop	  or	  add	  a	  repeated	  STR	  unit	  when	  replicating	  an	  STR	  
fragment.	  	  The	  Markov	  chain	  process	  forms	  a	  random	  pattern	  of	  fragment	  lengths	  centered	  
about	  the	  primary	  allele	  length.	  	  This	  PCR	  stutter	  pattern	  is	  far	  more	  pronounced	  with	  the	  
mono-­‐	  or	  di-­‐nucleotide	  repeat	  loci	  used	  in	  genetics,	  and	  attenuated	  somewhat	  with	  the

            The	  stutter	  amount	  increases	  with	  the	  number	  of	  repeats,	  and	  can	  be	  modeled	  as	  a	  
regression	  line.	  	  Let	  !x 	  be	  the	  number	  of	  repeat	  units,	  and	  ! y 	  the	  stutter	  proportion.	  	  Then	  
the	  linear	  model	  relating	  increasing	  stutter	  amount	  to	  repeat	  length	  at	  a	  locus	  is:

Differential	  Degradation	  


Polymerase	  requires	  a	  connected	  DNA	  fragment	  in	  order	  to	  make	  a	  copy.	  	  One	  or	  more	  
breaks	  in	  a	  DNA	  sequence	  will	  prevent	  PCR	  copying.	  	  The	  chance	  of	  having	  no	  breaks	  in	  a	  
fragment	  (unimpeded	  copying)	  follows	  an	  exponential	  decay	  curve	  in	  the	  fragment	  length	  
variable,	  with	  a	  decay	  rate	  proportional	  to	  the	  density	  of	  DNA	  breaks.	  	  	  
             Since	  TrueAllele	  models	  the	  DNA	  mass	  and	  variation	  of	  each	  experiment	  separately,	  
no	  additional	  modeling	  is	  needed	  when	  DNA	  degradation	  or	  inhibition	  is	  the	  same	  for	  all	  
contributors.	  	  However,	  when	  there	  is	  differential	  degradation	  between	  the	  different	  
contributors,	  the	  decay	  rate	  of	  each	  contributor’s	  DNA	  can	  be	  determined	  by	  logarithmic	  
modeling	  of	  the	  exponential	  process.	  	  	  
             Let	  !x 	  be	  allele	  size,	  ! y 	  contributor	  allele	  amount,	  and	   yeff 	  the	  effective	  contributor
                                                                                                       !
amount	  following	  DNA	  degradation.	  	  Then	  the	  linear	  model	  relating	  effective	  allele	  amount

Hierarchical	  Modeling	  


TrueAllele	  models	  variables	  hierarchically,	  subdividing	  them	  by	  experiment.	  	  Thus	  one	  
parameter	  can	  expand	  into	  many	  parameters,	  one	  for	  each	  STR	  locus	  experiment,	  and	  
another	  one	  for	  the	  group.	  	  This	  expansion	  of	  variables	  permits	  modeling	  that	  is	  more	  
customized	  to	  the	  data,	  yielding	  more	  accurate	  answers.	  	  	  
            For	  example,	  contributor	  mixture	  weights	  are	  determined	  for	  each	  locus	  experiment	  
as	  the	  set	  of	  variables	   {w l } ,	  and	  also	  for	  the	  DNA	  template	  as	  group	  variable	   w .

Statistical	  Computing	  


The	  joint	  probability	  distribution	  is	  fully	  specified	  as	  the	  product	  of	  the	  likelihood	  and	  prior	  
distributions.	  	  Using	  a	  Metropolis-­‐Hastings	  sampler,	  we	  iteratively	  draw	  from	  the	  posterior	  
probability	  distributions	  of	   {g k,l } ,	   {w l } ,	   { ml } ,	   w ,	   σ 2 ,	   τ 2 ,	   ψ 2 	  and	  other	  variables	  using

Markov	  chain	  Monte	  Carlo	  (MCMC)	  computer	  methods.	  	  
            Once	  beyond	  the	  initial	  burn	  in	  phase,	  the	  Markov	  chain	  samples	  from	  the	  joint	  
posterior	  probability	  distribution.	  	  Marginalizing	  these	  posterior	  samples	  to	  each	  genotype

probability	  functions	   q(x) 	  for	  the	  genotypes.	  	  	  	  


Match	  Statistic	  


The	  likelihood	  ratio	  (LR)	  is	  the	  information	  gained	  in	  the	  hypothesis	  H	  odds	  by	  having	  
observed	  data	  

                                                           LR =
                                                                       (
                                                                    O H dQ , d R , dS     )
                                                                           O(H )

Here,	  hypothesis	  H	  is	  that	  the	  suspect	  contributed	  to	  the	  DNA	  evidence,	  and	  the	  DNA	  data	  
comprises	  the	  questioned	  evidence	   dQ ,	  the	  reference	  population	  allele	  frequencies	   d R 	  and	  

suspect	  profile	   dS .	  	  
            Standard	  Bayesian	  rearrangements	  tell	  us	  that	  the	  LR	  can	  also	  be	  written	  as	  the	  
ratio	  of	  conditional	  probabilities	  

                                                          LR =
                                                                       {
                                                                   Pr dQ H , d R , dS     }
                                                                       {
                                                                   Pr dQ H , d R , dS     }
where	   H 	  is	  the	  alternative	  hypothesis	  that	  someone	  else	  contributed	  to	  the	  evidence.	  	  
            Suppose	  that	  there	  is	  uncertainty	  in	  the	  evidence	  genotype	  having	  pmf	   q ( x ) or	  in	  the

suspect	  genotype	  with	  pmf	   s ( x ) .	  	  Then	  this	  genotype	  uncertainty	  is	  expressed	  in	  the	  LR	  as

                                                                 ∑ λ ( x) ⋅ s( x)
                                                                           Q
                                                            LR =     x∈G

                                                                 ∑ λ ( x) ⋅ r ( x)
                                                                           Q
                                                                     x∈G


where	   λQ ( x ) 	  is	  the	  likelihood	  function	  of	  the	  evidence	  genotype	  Q	  and	   r ( x ) 	  is	  the	  pmf	  of

reference	  population	  genotype.	  	  
            Bayes	  theorem	  lets	  us	  rewrite	  this	  ratio	  of	  likelihood	  sums	  as	  a	  numerically	  
equivalent	  sum	  of	  posterior	  genotype	  probability	  product	  ratios.	  	  Probability	  can	  be	  more	  
intuitive	  and	  easier	  to	  explain	  than	  likelihood.	  	  	  
                                                                          q( x) ⋅ s( x)
                                                             LR = ∑
                                                                      x∈G    r ( x)

match	  probability	  to	  coincidence.	  	  	  
	  
Co-­‐ancestry	  Correction	  
	  
The	  LR	  for	  the	  hypothesis	  that	  a	  person	  contributed	  their	  DNA	  to	  evidence	  items	  1	  and	  2	  is	  
calculated	  from	  genotype	  probability	  distributions	  via:	  	  

                                                          ∑ λ (x)⋅ λ (x)⋅ π (x)
                                                                      1                2       θ
                                                    LR =       x∈G
                                                                                    	  
                                                         ∑ ∑ λ (x)⋅ λ (y)⋅ π (x, y)
                                                                          1                2       θ
                                                         x∈G    y∈G

                                           003646
Abstract



Computers have revolutionized DNA evidence interpretation, replacing guesswork by sound

statistical inference. Probabilistic reasoning resolves complex DNA mixtures, extracting

contributor genotypes whose uncertainty is expressed through probability. Information theory

can tell us much about these “probabilistic” genotypes, even before making a comparison to

calculate a likelihood ratio (LR). A genotype’s distribution of possible LR outcomes, under prior

or posterior probability assumptions, shows the power and breadth of its match possibilities.

       Genotype LR distributions can be rapidly computed by convolving independent locus

distributions. The tail probability of the non-contributor distribution gives the chance that the

evidence against a random person is as strong as it is against the suspect. This LR error is a

generalized random match probability (RMP) for uncertain genotypes. A sexual assault case

example applies these LR and RMP concepts to DNA mixture evidence and database search.

       While the LR summarizes evidence, the RMP estimates error. Both statistical measures

assist a trier of fact in understanding DNA evidence.
