The three-story rental house at 1122 King Road in Moscow, Idaho was home to Xana
Kernodle, Kaylee Goncalves, and Madison Mogen. Xana Kernodle and Ethan Chapin
were dating, and he was sleeping over at the house that night. It was also home to
Dylan Mortensen and Bethany Funke, neither of whom were reportedly approached or
harmed during this incident. The homicides are reported to have occurred on November
13, 2022, in the early hours of the morning, just after 4am.

This history, context, and reported information are necessary and foundational to the
forensic conclusions offered within this report. This is in compliance with the national
protocols for death investigation established by The NIJ (2011, 2013, & 2024). It is also
in compliance best scientific practices established in the published scientific literature
cited in this report.


II. INVESTIGATIVE & FORENSIC ISSUES
The following investigative red flags are evident in this case, requiring further
investigative attention and resolution:

A. Crime Scene Security / Physical Evidence: As explain in the NIJ Protocols for Crime
   Scene Investigation (2013) and Death Investigation (2011 & 2024), crime scene
   security and establishing and evidentiary chain of custody are essential for the
   preservation of Evidence Integrity. Evidence Integrity is demonstrated by adherence
   to basic protocols associated with establishing a reliable Chain of Custody for
   evidence present and the scene; the protection of physical evidence prior to and
   during its collection; and its protection during transportation storage — to enable
   competent examination, testing, and interpretation by qualified forensic personnel. It
   also implicitly refers to any failure to collect, protect, and/ or test essential items of
   evidence. In scientific examinations, Evidence Integrity and the underlying Chain of
   Custody for any item of physical evidence may not be assumed. These must be
   documented and established — otherwise, reliable interpretations and
   reconstructions are not possible5.

    In the present case, some law enforcement efforts were made to secure the crime
    scene subsequent to the arrival of crime scene processing personnel, to include
    stationing officers at the front and rear doors. However, a number of security failures
    are evident. These failures had a harmful impact on Chain of Custody and related
    Evidence Integrity. These failures, which prevent certainty with respect to who had
    access to the crime scene and when — prior to processing efforts — include the
    following:

   1. 8 Hours Unsecured: The scene was not secure for approximately 8hrs prior to
      the arrival of law enforcement. During this extended timeframe, the remaining

   the home without their movements being documented. This reality has the

   evidence dynamics are not noted as detrimental in subsequent collection or

2. The Activity of Dylan Mortenson & Bethany Funke: Dylan Mortensen and
   Bethany Funke were not approached or attacked during this incident. This
   despite being awake and texting with each other at the time (4am) — with Dylan
   reporting that she saw an intruder outside of her bedroom door. Their digital
   activity appears to have continued after this, indicating that both were awake,
   texting, and making phone calls before their reported activity in relation to calling
   friends, family and eventually 911.

   Emily Alandt was contacted by Dylan Mortenson at around 11:50am. Emily was
   reportedly asked to come over and check on the house with her boyfriend,
   Hunter Johnson. Hunter Johnson did so as described below.

   Prior to the arrival of Emily and Hunter, Dylan Mortenson and Bethany Funke
   had unfettered access to all areas of the residence but reported not leaving their
   Bethany’s room — after Dylan went to Bethany’s room to join her. It is unclear
   whether law enforcement fully investigated and established the activity in the
   home during this 8hr interval. Or why police / EMS were not called, despite
   concerns about one of their housemates being passed out and non-responsive.

3. The Activity of Hunter Johnson: After the arrival of Emily Alandt and Hunter
   Johnson, 911 was called (11:56am). When officers arrived on scene minutes
   later, they encountered Hunter Johnson inside the residence. Hunter reported
   that he had arrived about 15-20 minutes prior to law enforcement and entered
   the home at the request of his girlfriend, Emily Alandt. Johnson immediately
   admitted to entering and moving around within the house, moving a knife from
   the kitchen to the beer pong table on the second floor to be used for his own self-
   defense, and checking the pulse of one of the victims. Law enforcement
   documented this activity, however is unknown what other movements throughout
   the home occurred that could have altered the existing evidence. These
   evidence dynamics are not noted as detrimental in subsequent collection or
   examination efforts, despite having a negative impact on Chain of Custody and
   related Evidence Integrity.

4. Evidence Dynamics / Multiple Officers: On officer body-cams, multiple officers
   can be observed entering the first floor entrance, moving through the different
   rooms, up both sets of stairs, and walking around on different floors. While
   somewhat unavoidable, these movements throughout the home could have
   altered and even obliterated existing physical evidence. These evidence

B. Crime Scene Security / Interview & Suspect Integrity at the Scene: A basic
   consideration with respect to preserving the integrity of witness and suspect
   interviews is the immediate separation of persons at the scene. This helps to
   prevent collusion, and narrative manipulation, before or in the moment of a
   preliminary law enforcement interview. Law enforcement personnel failed with
   respect to this basic duty of care. Specific failures, which prevent reliability with
   respect the statements taken at the scene and resulted in the abandonment of
   physical evidence, include the following:

   1. As observed on law enforcement body-cams, all witnesses were allowed to
      gather together outside on the street for an extended period of time, within law
      enforcement view — but well out of earshot.

   2. As observed on law enforcement body-cams, none of the surviving witnesses
      from inside the home were properly interviewed on scene by responding officers.
      This is generally done to get a preliminary or rough version of events by those
      who observed it firsthand. It also better informs the safe entry of law
      enforcement, the search for others that may be or should be in the home, and
      evidence search / preservation efforts. Without this information, it is difficult to
      separate victims from suspects once inside the scene, the result of which could
      be additional tragedy.

   3. As observed on law enforcement body-cams, the witnesses gathered outside of
      the crime scene were allowed to leave the scene by law enforcement prior to
      being subject to a preliminary interview and identity confirmation.

C. Abandoned Forensic Evidence: As observed on law enforcement body-cams, and
   later law enforcement reports, there was negligent failure and professional
   abandonment with respect to reported crime scene evidence. This extreme
   professional abandonment — which evidences a lack of crime scene education,
   training, and experience — include the following:

   1. As observed on law enforcement body-cams, all of the witnesses, including the
      surviving housemates Dylan Mortensen and Bethany Funke, were allowed to
      leave the scene by law enforcement without being examined for blood evidence,
      injury or trauma; without the examination or collection of their clothing or shoes;
      and without checking their persons for items of evidence. This is necessary for
      both the identification and documentation of potential physical evidence, and
      negative documentation with respect to its absence. This is nothing short of
      professional abandonment of pertinent crime scene evidence.

   The trashcan, toilet, and bathtub/shower should have carefully documented in

3. As evidenced in crime scene photos and evidentiary reports, law enforcement

   clothing from inside the washer/dryer, the trash, the inside of the shower stall, or

   the 3rd floor bathroom. All of these items should have carefully documented in
   situ and photographed, collected into evidence, examined for bloody transfer and
   clean-up efforts, and tested for DNA.

5. Based on a review of the provided evidence, none of the areas in the home, to
   include areas of potential clean-up, were examined with presumptive chemical
   reagents such as Luminol or Bluestar to search the scene for additional blood
   evidence. Such field testing is both standard an essential with respect to in-door
   cases involving even low levels of blood evidence or potential blood-flow / blood
   transfer.

6. In early January of 2023, the Defense intervened to preserve and collect
   extensive physical evidence left behind at the crime scene and prevent its
   destruction by law enforcement. Much of this evidence had received observable
   blood transfer evidence in the form of contact smears, drops, and spatter. To be
   clear, law enforcement negligently failed to preserve and collect a long list of
   items from victim bedrooms, other bedrooms, and the house in general. They
   also inappropriately released personal items belonging to the victims and
   surviving household members before independent examination efforts could be
   made, as indicated by the Supplemental Narrative provided below:

7. At the instruction of the Defense, law enforcement returned to the scene on
   1/6/23 and collected 10 items, to include bed frames, mattresses, pillows, and
   blankets covered with blood transfer evidence. These items had been left behind
   at the scene during law enforcement processing efforts and were scheduled to
   be destroyed along with the house.

   dog “Murphy” in Kaylee’s room, on her bed, calmly sitting. The dog did not have

E. Suspect Bias: A review of investigative efforts indicates that none of those at the
   scene, or from inside the house, were questioned or investigated as though they
   were a suspect. The vast majority of investigative efforts by law enforcement (e.g.,
   Moscow PD and The FBI) focused on the theory that there was only one suspect,
   that this suspect entered without permission, and that this suspect did not reside in
   the home.

   Once Bryan Kohberger became a suspect, no other investigative avenues were
   pursued. All of Kohberger´s activity, before and after the homicides, became a
   matter of intense law enforcement focus and was subsequently viewed through a
   theory of guilt. Notably, none of the defendant’s activity investigated by law
   enforcement has been found to be criminal or suggestive of attempting to evade
   criminal charges.

      identity the suspect vehicle(s) in this case. The failure to be absolutely clear and
      forthcoming about this evident fact would be evidence of bias.

   2. The Defendant’s vehicle is a white 2015 Hyundai Elantra, License Plate
      CFB8708. This was theorized by law enforcement to have been a suspect
      vehicle associated with this case. It was subsequently seized by the
      Pennsylvania State Police, transported to the Moscow Police Department, and
      examined.

   3. As will be discussed in the subsequent section of this report, the suspect(s)
      involved in committing these homicides would have been covered in blood as a
      result of the extraordinary amount of blood spatter and necessary blood
      transfers. This includes hands, arms, legs, feet, and related clothing — which
      would have transferred onto and into any suspect(s) vehicle in relation to
      opening doors, entering seats, adjusting the seats or mirrors, closing doors,
      inserting keys, using the gear shift, and using the steering wheel. All off these
      being necessary actions or movements for the successful operation of a motor
      vehicle. These transfers can be microscopic, and can be detected using
      presumptive chemical reagents such as Luminol and Bluestar.

   4. Despite an extensive and exhaustive forensic examination of the Defendant’s
      vehicle for bloody clothing, blood transfer, and other evidence related to these
      crimes — down to the metal — none was found. This has essentially excluded
      the Defendant’s vehicle as being related to the commission of these crimes. The
      failure to be absolutely clear and forthcoming about this evident fact would be
      evidence of bias.

Additional investigative and forensic issues are present, however these are among the
most relevant and concerning.

A. Points of Entry / Exit: Aside from the windows, which are impractical or evidently

IV. MODUS OPERANDI
Modus Operandi (MO) is a Latin term that means method of operating. It refers to the
manner in which a crime has been committed. A criminal’s Modus Operandi is
comprised of choices and behaviors that are intended to assist in the completion and
concealment of a crime (Turvey, 2022). Black’s Law Dictionary (Black, 1990, p.1004)
translates the phrase modus operandi as “method of operation or doing things,” and
states that it is “used by police and criminal investigators to describe the particular
method of a criminal’s activity.” Specifically, a Modus Operandi is comprised of
individual and heuristic choices and behaviors that are intended to assist in the
completion of a crime (see generally Atchereley, 1913; Turvey, 2022; Weston & Wells,
1974).

The physical and behavioral evidence evident in this crime evidence the following
elements related to Modus Operandi:

A. Planning and Precaution: The elements of Planning and Precaution demonstrated in
   the Modus Operandi of this crime are low skill with respect to planning and
   execution, and high skill with respect to precaution.

   1. Planning: Whatever planning may have taken place with respect to this crime, it
      resulted in an excessive number of victims with an excess of bloody transfer and
      bloody clothing on the part of the suspects. This took additional time to both
      effect and clean up before they could leave.


                                                                        Brent E. Turvey, PhD
                                                           CSA: Idaho vs. Bryan C. Kohberger
                                                                               Page 19 of 25

                                          004044
   2.   Precautionary Acts: The precautionary acts in this case include the execution of
        living witnesses; the clean-up of bloody hands, feet / foot-ware and clothing
        before leaving; and the disposal of said clothing along with the weapons used.
        Direct evidence of this clean-up can be found in at least some of the dilute blood
        transfer which was located in different areas of the home. Indirect evidence
        includes the absence of bloody transfer from feet and hands, despite the
        movement of suspects within the homes, the necessary opening of doors, and
        the absence of bloody footwear patterns at the scene in general. All of this would
        have required an extensive amount of time at the scene to clean, perhaps hours,
        which is inconsistent with the State's theory that these crimes were committed
        within a time interval less than 15-20 minutes, subsequent to 4am.

B. Number of Suspects: At least two suspects were involved in this attack. This is
   indicated by the fact that multiple weapons were used against Kaylee; that multiple
   types of lethal force were used against Kaylee; and that Ethan and Xana appear to
   have been attacked at the same time. This is inconsistent with the State's theory
   that these crimes were committed solely by one individual.

C. Posing: As mentioned prior, posing is evident in the present case. This is based on
   the following facts and evidence: This refers to intentionally arranging the scene for
   effect. In the present case, the bodies of Kaylee and Madison were posed together
   after the lethal attacks suffered by both, and then they covered together with a
   comforter (See photo below).




                                                                         Brent E. Turvey, PhD
                                                            CSA: Idaho vs. Bryan C. Kohberger
                                                                               Page 20 of 25

                                           004045
D. Staging: Crime Scene Staging refers to an attempt to confuse or misdirect a law
   enforcement investigation by altering, fabricating, or planting evidence in relation to
   a crime scene (Chisum & Turvey, 2012). In the present case, a Ka-Bar Knife Sheath
   was discovered in the crime scene by law enforcement. Evidence of staging with
   respect to this item of evidence is as follows:

   1.   The sheath was found precariously placed just slightly under the body of
        Madison Mogen, and partially covered by the comforter that was placed atop the
        midsection of her body by the suspects. It could not have fallen accidentally into
        this location (See photo below).




   2.   The sheath was new and unused, as indicated by the absence of damage or
        wear to the leather.

   3.   The sheath was face down, and had received only a few areas of minute blood
        spatter (impact or aspirated) while resting atop a sheet with significant impact
        spatter all around. The inconsistency of blood spatter dispersion and density
        indicate transfers occurring at different times, under different conditions, with
        different levels of intensity.

   4. The sheath was placed at that location without receiving bloody transfer from the
      hands or fingers of the suspect that did it. This means it was done after the
      attacks / posing, but also after the suspect had washed their hands, subsequent
      to lean-up efforts and the scene (See photos below).




                                                                          Brent E. Turvey, PhD
                                                             CSA: Idaho vs. Bryan C. Kohberger
                                                                                Page 21 of 25

                                           004046
                      Brent E. Turvey, PhD
         CSA: Idaho vs. Bryan C. Kohberger
                            Page 22 of 25

004047
E. Primary Target: The Primary target in this case was Kaylee Goncalves. She was
   specifically targeted by the suspects, and the rest of the victims in the home were
   collateral. This is based on the following facts and evidence:

   1. Kaylee’s room was the least convenient and most risky to access in the home,
      yet she and Madison were attacked first.

   2. The attack suffered by Kaylee was the most extensive, involving the most
      injuries, and was therefore the most time consuming.

   3. Kaylee was stabbed repeatedly in the face until she was unrecognizable. No
      other victim suffered this amount of close up facial attention or damage.

   4. Kaylee suffered multiple types of lethal force (stabbing, blunt force trauma, and
      asphyxiation). All other victims suffered only one form of lethal force. This level of
      unnecessary close interaction and brutality are characteristic of primary targets
      in cases motivated by anger and rage.

F. Motive: The physical and behavioral evidence in this case evidence an Anger-
   Retaliatory motivation. As explained in Turvey (2022), this is: “evidenced by crime
   scene behaviors that involve a great deal of rage, either toward a specific person,
   group, or institution, or a symbol of either”. It is also evidenced by what may be
   referred to as evidence of overkill — injury beyond that needed to cause death,
   involving the repeated infliction of injury subsequent to the application of lethal force.
   In combination with multiple types of lethal force against one victim and not the
   others, this motive is all but confirmed.


Should new evidence become available, this examiner would necessarily
reconsider any of the related findings in this report.

       - Forensic examination conducted of related evidence.
       - Crime reconstruction established an alternate suspect and disproved law enforcement case
       theories.
       CRIMINAL: All charges dismissed. Forensic findings used to assist with the release of defendant
       in 2020 after five years waiting for trial. Forensic findings subsequently used to assist with
       motion to dismiss all charges in 2021.

37. 2021-2022: Oregon v. Kiah Lawson
       Forensic Examination: false report of sexual assault determination
       - Assisted with development of crime reconstruction and cross-examination to help prep case
         and elicit exculpatory evidence from state’s witnesses.
       CRIMINAL: Defense Attorney Client / Case Dismissed prior to trial (January, 2022)

38. 2021-2022: Coahuila v. Sergio Armando Mitre (MEXICO) - Double Femicide

       former pitcher for the New York Yankees
       - Reprocessed crime scene; discovered new physical physical evidence; exhumed body and
         participated in necropsy; provided expert report and findings; helped develop trial strategy.
       CRIMINAL: Attorney General’s Office, Coahuila / Defendant convicted

On January 28, 2023, I accompanied you and members of your staff, as well as Matthew Noedel,

                                                  2



                                               004096
                                         Background


Kaylee Goncalves (age 21), Xana Kernodle (age 20) and Madison Mogen (age 21) were students
at the University of Idaho who lived in an off-campus six bedroom house at 1122 King Road,
Moscow. They had two other roommates, Bethany G. Funke and Dylan Mortensen. The sixth
bedroom was vacant. Ethan Chapin (age 20) was Xana Kernodle's boyfriend and frequently
stayed at the residence. The top (third) floor of the house included two bedrooms, one occupied
by Madison and the other by Kaylee and her dog, Murphy, and a bathroom. The second floor
included bedrooms occupied by Xana and Dylan, a kitchen, living space and bathroom. A
sliding glass door in the kitchen led to a back patio. The bottom floor included Bethany's room,
the unoccupied room, bathroom, a locked mechanical room and a front door to the outside.

On the evening of November 12, 2022 Xana and Ethan were seen at a party at Ethan's fraternity.
Madison and Kaylee had gone to a sports bar and were seen ordering food at a food truck at
approximately 1:30 a.m. on the morning of November 13, 2022. Bethany Funke reported that
Madison and Kaylee returned home at approximately 2:00 a.m. and that she and Madison let
Kaylee's dog out. Hunter Johnson, a friend of the roommates, texted Ethan at 1:21 a.m. and
received a response at 1:43 a.m. Hunter reported to the police that he had been to the house the
previous evening and found no one home. DoorDash delivered food ordered by Xana at 3:59
a.m. Neighborhood videos revealed a suspect vehicle making multiple slow passes by the
residence between 3:30 a.m. and 4:07 a.m. and at 4:20 a.m. the vehicle left the scene.

According to Emily Alandt, Xana's friend and Hunter's girlfriend, Dylan, called her at
approximately 11:51 a.m. on the morning of November 13, 2022, in distress, and told her that at
approximately 4:00 a.m. she had seen a man in black and that she had heard Kaylee scream.
Hunter came to the house at "sometime after 11:00 am" and entered with a code. The door to
Xana's second floor room was not completely open. Hunter observed Xana on the floor and
Ethan on the bed. He told Bethany and Dylan, who had been in Bethany's room on the first floor
and were unharmed, to call the police. A911 call originating from Bethany Funke's phone
reported that "someone was passed out." Hunter did not go up to the third floor. Law
enforcement and emergency medical personnel responded and death was pronounced without
resuscitation attempts. The bodies of Madison and Kaylee were found in Madison's bed. A knife
sheath, subsequently identified as that of a Ka-Bar knife, was discovered in the bed. All four of
the deceased students had multiple sharp force injuries. Kaylee's dog was on the bed in her
room, unharmed.

Dylan reported that she thought she had heard the dog whimpering and someone crying in the
early morning hours of November 13, 2022. She heard a commotion, and locked her bedroom
door. In a subsequent interview Dylan stated that she saw an unknown person approximately five
feet away wearing a ski mask and "all black" in the kitchen at approximately 4:00 a.m., which
was close to her bedroom door, walking toward the sliding door. She was scared but did not call
the police, rather she went downstairs to the first floor to sleep in Bethany's room.

Bryan Christopher Kohberger was subsequently identified as a suspect in the murders. A single
source of male DNA was found by the Idaho State Police Lab on the button snap of the knife


                                                3


                                             004097
sheath. He was arrested on December 30, 2022 at his parents' home in Pennsylvania. Kohberger
was a 28-year-old Ph.D. criminology student at Washington State University who lived in an
apartment in Pullman, Washington. He had driven home with his father for the Christmas break. A
cheek swab taken from Bryan Kohberger was a statistical match only to the DNA evidence found
on the button snap of the knife sheath, although ISP Forensics also swabbed other areas of the
sheath.




According to a report of Detective Dani Vargas of the Moscow Police Department, members of
the prosecution team met with Dr. Veena Singh at the Spokane County Medical Examiner's
Office on June 28, 2023 and showed her an exemplar full-sized Ka-Bar knife U.S. Marine
Corps Fighting Knife. The report of the interview indicated that "Dr. Singh stated the shape
and size of the Ka-Bar knife was consistent as being the weapon which could have caused the
injuries on all four of the victims" and "described some injuries depicted that the strength of
the weapon itself, and the force used, would have been great."


                                   Postmortem Examinations


Postmortem examinations were performed on the bodies of Ethan Chapin, Kaylee Goncalves,
Xana Kernodle and Madison Mogen on November 16, 2022 by Dr. Veena Singh at the
Spokane County, WA Office of the Medical Examiner. The cause of death of all four decedents
was listed as multiple sharp force injuries. Additionally, in the "Opinion" section of the report of
the examination of Kaylee Goncalves it is stated that "blunt force injuries of the head and
asphyxial injuries were listed as significant contributors to death." Total body radiographs
(Lodox) revealed no metallic foreign bodies such as the tip of a knife.

There was no scene or autopsy evidence of sexual assaults. Swabs were taken at the autopsies of
multiple of body surfaces and the oral and anal cavities. Additionally, a penile swab was taken
from Ethan and vaginal swabs from the three women. Fingernail clippings were obtained from
all decedents. These items were tured over to the Moscow Police Department.

In Coroner Mabbutt's death certificate abstracts, the sections "Describe How Injury Occurred"
for each decedent are completed as follows:

       Ethan Chapin: Stabbed by large knife multiple times
       Kaylee Goncalves: Multiple stab wounds subdural bleeds asphyxial injuries
       Xana Kernodle: Multiple stab wounds on head, chest and arms
       Madison Mogel: Stabbed multiple times with large knife

It is notable that none of the medical examiner files included any notes or diagrams, which made
correlation between the written descriptions and the autopsy photographs difficult with some of

                                      General Information


A stab wound is by definition a sharp force injury that is deeper in its depth in the body than its
length on the skin surface, although this definition becomes arbitrary when the path of the knife
is stopped by a heavy bone such as the skull. Stab wounds have sharp margins with fine, if any,
marginal abrasions unless the inflicting knife is dull. In contrast, an incised wound, or cut, is
longer on the skin surface than its depth in the body and also has clean cut edges. The
importance of this distinction is that the morphology of a stab wound may reflect the
configurating of the inflicting instrument, while the morphology of an incised wound does not.
The only information that an incised wound will provide about the weapon is that it had a sharp
edge. Many sharp force injuries have components of both stab and incised wounds due to motion
of the assailant and/or the victim.

Many stab wounds have a gaping appearance on the skin due to the skin's elastic fibers
(Langer's lines) that pull the edges of the wound apart. In order to properly evaluate a stab
wound, it is essential to re-approximate the edges of the wound to release the tension. When re-
approximated, the measurement of the length of a stab wound will more accurately reflect the
width of the blade of the knife at the point that it penetrated the body. Additionally, with a stab
wound inflicted by a knife of significant thickness, it may be possible to distinguish whether the
inflicting knife was single-edged or double-edged if one of the ends is squared off or blunted.
and the other end is sharp or pointed. However, with a thin knife such as a steak knife this
determination is usually not possible.

The determination of whether a stab wound was inflicted by a serrated or a non-serrated knife is
most often not possible from the morphology of the wound unless the serrated portion of the
blade was dragged tangentially across the adjacent skin. When a knife enters and exits the body
perpendicularly, evidence of serrations will be obliterated.

It is important to distinguish an incised wound from laceration, which is a tear in tissue
                                                        a




resulting from a blunt impact that caused a shearing or crushing force. Most lacerations have
abraded or contused margins rather than the sharp margins of a sharp force injury. Additionally,
lacerations are characterized by bridging of tissue within the depth of the wound due to differing
strengths of differing types of soft tissues that result in incomplete separation of the stronger
tissues.

                        My Opinions and the Bases and Reasons Thereof


My opinions in this matter are based on my review of the above-listed materials, as well as my
training and experience in the fields of medicine and forensic pathology.


                                                  10


                                               004104
Sharp Force Injuries:

It is my opinion, to a reasonable degree of medical certainty and in agreement with the opinion
of the autopsy pathologist, that the causes of death of Ethan Chapin, Kaylee Goncalves, Xana
Kernodle and Madison Mogen were multiple sharp injuries.

In general, I agree that the majority of the wounds are consistent with the estimation of the width
and thickness of the blade (approximately 1-3/16 to 1-1/4 inch in width and approximately 5/32
to 3/16 in thickness) as opined by Dr. Singh in her reports of the postmortem examinations.

However, it is further my opinion, to a reasonable degree of medical certainty, that not all of the
sharp force injuries observed on the decedents could have been inflicted by the knife described
by Dr. Singh. Madison Mogen had one sharp force injury, Kaylee Goncalves one and Xana
Kernodle at least three with configurations that differ from Dr. Singh's estimation of the
measurements of the inflicting knife. These wounds are also described above in the summation
of the decedents' injuries.

Blunt Force Injuries:

There are other injuries that are inconsistent with being caused by a knife and therefore also
suggest the use of another weapon(s). Most notable are the two lacerations of Kaylee's scalp and
the associated occipital skull fracture. These are blunt force injuries which would necessitate
with significant weight to fracture the heavy occipital bone.




                                                   17


                                                 004111
It is unlikely that that these injuries were inflicted with an assailant using the end of the handle of
a knife having the configuration of the exemplar knife. The wounds do not have a circular
configuration as they would have if the base of the knife struck the head perpendicularly nor a
curvilinear configuration as they would if the circular rim of the base struck the head.




Kaylee also had extensive bruising on her face. Additionally, the patterned bruises on her peri-
orbital skin and her oral injuries were the result of blunt trauma, with the damage to the mucosal
surface of her lower lip contributed to by pressure of the lip against the teeth. These findings are
consistent with a blunt object being pressed across her lower face and/or possible gagging.



                                                  18


                                                004112
Asphyxial Injuries:

Lastly, as noted by Dr. Singh, Kaylee's ocular and oral petechiae are consistent with an
asphyxial component to her death, such as suffocation or strangulation. Petechiae are pinpoint
hemorrhages produced by rupture of small blood vessels due to mechanical occlusion and
therefore over distension. Although nonspecific findings, ocular and oral petechiae are a red flag
for neck compression.

                                              004113
An unsigned document titled Behavioral Unit of FBI ViCAP Re Idaho Students ViCAP
NUMBER: 2022ZZP00001 opined that Kaylee was sleeping at the time of the attack and by blitz
was hit with a hand, fist or clubbing instrument and stabbed/cut. Ethan and Madison were also
believed to have been awakened and stabbed/cut. The document opines that Xana encountered
the assailant in the house after having been on social media shortly before and was cut and
stabbed. All four victims are described as having "'puncture/torture wounds." The document
describes symbolic acts that in many of the wounds on all the victims were nearly identical in
shape and location.


                                         Conclusions


Based on the above described observations and measurements, it is my opinion, to a reasonable
degree of medical certainty, that some of the sharp and blunt force inflicted on Kaylee
Goncalves, Xana Kernodle and Madison Mogen are not consistent with having been caused by a
knife with the dimensions estimated by Dr. Singh in her reports of the postmortem examinations.
Additionally, Kaylee's blunt force and asphyxial injuries were not caused by a cutting
implement. This indicates that there were at least two knives used, one of which was narrower
than the configuration of the knife that caused the majority of the evaluable wounds, and a blunt
object or surface. This raises the likelihood that there was more than one assailant involved in
the homicides.

The likelihood of there having been more than one perpetrator is supported by the fact that it
seems highly improbable that one assailant would be able control and kill four young, healthy
adults in the extremely short time frame during which the killings occurred that has been
established by investigative information. Additionally, the lack of blood and/or DNA evidence in
Bryan Kohberger's vehicle and his apartment suggests that there was another vehicle involved.
The multiple wounds sustained by the victims, including some that would have resulted in
arterial bleeding, would have left blood on the clothing and bodies of the perpetrator(s) or any
protective coverings that may have been worn, the disposition of which would have further
lengthened the time frame involved in the killings.

With regard to the unsigned document titled Behavioral Unit of FBI ViCAP Re Idaho Students
in which is it opined that the victims had torture wounds and that there was symbolic meaning to
many of the wounds, I respectfully disagree. While I do agree that the attacks were surprise/blitz
in nature, in my opinion the locations of the wounds were the results of opportunity in that they
were inflicted in body areas that were exposed on the victims who were in bed and when they
were awakened.

However, the superficial incised wounds of Kaylee's and Madison's anterior neck merit
comment. Kaylee's incised neck wounds are shown below on the left. The incised wounds on
Madison's neck are pictured below on the right. They are even more superficial than those on
Kaylee's neck and are described as being minimally hemorrhagic. The superficial nature of these

                                                20


                                              004114
wounds is very unusual. The skin is the toughest tissue of the neck until the spine is reached.
Once the skin is breached, it takes much less force to cut through the underlying soft tissues, so
such wounds are usually deep. It is difficult to understand how these wounds were produced in
the course of the obvious struggle and motion involved in the deaths of these women. It can be
postulated that these wounds were deliberately inflicted superficially, which would have
necessitated precise movements and would have further lengthened the length of time involved
in the killings.




                                        My Qualifications


I am a physician, licensed to practice medicine in the state of Florida. I also hold inactive
licenses in the states of Massachusetts, New York, and New Jersey. 1 am currently employed as
the District Medical Examiner for Florida's District 5, serving Lake, Sumter, Marion, Hernando
and Citrus Counties and the Interim District Medical Examiner for District 24, serving Seminole
County. I am Board Certified by the American Board of Pathology in the specialties of anatomic
pathology, hematopathology and in forensic pathology. I have previously served as the Director
of the Divisions of Anatomic Pathology and Hematopathology in the Department of Pathology
and Laboratory Medicine at the Albany Medical Center, and I was an adjunct full Professor of
Pathology at the Albany Medical College. Between 1991 and 2001 I also served up to 20
counties in upstate New York as a coroner's pathologist. I stepped down from the directorship
position at Albany Medical Center in 1996 to pursue full time forensic pathology. In 1997 I took
the position of Chief Medical Examiner for Rensselaer County, New York, and in 1999 I became
the Director of Forensic Medicine for the Medicolegal Investigation Unit of the New York State
Police. I relocated to Palm Beach County, Florida in 2001 where I served as the Deputy Chief
Medical Examiner and then to the District 21 Medical Examiner's Office in 2004, prior to
assuming the leadership position in the District 5 office in November of 2007 and in the District
 24 office in October of 2018. I am also currently the Chairperson of the Inspection and
Accreditation Committee of the National Association of Medical Examiners (NAME), which
accredits medical examiner and coroner offices nationally and internationally, and the
Chairperson of the Florida Medical Examiners Commission. For many years ] was a faculty
member of the National District Attorney's Association.
